Consistent hashing: when a backend holds per-key state or a local cache (cache shards, chat rooms, partitions).
avoidWhen: Avoid plain round robin when request cost varies a lot; a slow server keeps receiving its full share and its queue grows.
Avoid modulo hashing (hash mod N) when N changes: adding one server remaps most keys and empties caches.

rows: Blind to load and slow requests
Each balancer sees only its own counts
Key affinity, few keys move on resize

numbers.title: How many keys move when you add a server?
steps: Modulo hashing: a key stays put only if hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11, which is true for about 1 key in 11.
So about 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91% of keys move to a different server, and the cache hit rate collapses.
Consistent hashing: the new server takes over only its share of the ring, about 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9% of keys.
With 1 billion cached keys, that is about 910 million keys moving versus about 91 million.
numbers.result: Adding one server to ten moves about 91% of keys with modulo hashing but only about 9% with consistent hashing. That is why caches and partitions use consistent hashing.

india.title: Ticket checkout when some requests are slow
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: In a ticketing flow such as movie or train booking, most requests are quick (seat map, availability) but some are slow (payment confirmation that waits on a bank or UPI callback). Under round robin, a server that happens to collect several slow requests still gets its full share of new ones, its queue grows, and users see timeouts even though other servers are idle. Least connections or power of two choices sends new work to servers with fewer requests in flight, so slow calls do not pile up on one box. Separately, if seat-hold state is cached per show, consistent hashing on show ID keeps each show's state on one server, so adding servers before a big release moves only a small slice of shows.

pitfalls.trap: Choosing round robin for everything.
pitfalls.say: 'Request times vary here, so I'd use least connections or power of two choices so slow requests don't pile up.'

pitfalls.trap: Hashing with mod N on a cache tier that autoscales.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd use consistent hashing with virtual nodes so adding a server moves only about 1/N of the keys.'

deep.diagram:
round robin:    r1->A  r2->B  r3->C  r4->A ...
least conn:     A(12) B(3) C(7)   -> pick B
power of two:   sample {A,C} -> A(12) vs C(7) -> pick C
hash(user 42) -> ring position -> server B, every time
takeaways: Round robin suits uniform work; least connections and power of two choices handle uneven work.
Weights handle mixed server sizes.
Hashing gives key affinity; use consistent hashing so a resize moves about 1/N of keys, not most of them.
Watch for hot keys whenever you hash.

title: L4 vs L7 LB & Health Checks
objectives: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 routes by HTTP content (paths, headers, cookies).

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: L4 forwards TCP/UDP connections without reading payloads. L7 terminates HTTP, so it can route /api vs /static, do header-based canary routing and TLS termination.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 routes by HTTP content (paths, headers, cookies).

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Packet arrives” to “Forward to pool”, via “L4: inspect IP/port”.
steps: Packet arrives
L4: inspect IP/port
L7: parse HTTP
Match rule (path/header)
Forward to pool

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Choosing L4 when you need path-based routing, or L7 for non-HTTP protocols.

cards.title: Health checks
cards.body: The balancer probes each backend, for example GET /healthz every 5 s. After a few failures it stops routing there; after a few passes it adds it back. Active checks catch dead servers before users do; passive checks watch real responses for errors.

questions.prompt: Route /images to one pool and /api to another. Which balancer?

choices.label: An L4 balancer, because it is faster

questions.explanation: Only L7 reads the path.

questions.prompt: Which one needs an L4 balancer rather than L7?

choices.label: Canary routing on a request header
A custom TCP protocol for multiplayer game servers

questions.explanation: L7 balancers understand HTTP; a custom protocol needs plain TCP forwarding.

questions.prompt: A backend fails three health checks in a row. What does the balancer do?

choices.label: Removes it from DNS for every client
Sends it half its usual traffic
Stops sending it new requests until it passes checks again

questions.explanation: Balancers route around failures; restarting is the orchestrator’s job.

questions.prompt: Order an L7 routing decision.

items.label: Rule matched on path or header

questions.explanation: L7 must parse HTTP before it can match a rule.

questions.prompt: Pick a balancer for HTTPS web traffic that needs path routing.
constraints: TLS should end at the edge

rationaleOptions.label: L7 can read the path once it terminates TLS
L4 only sees IPs and ports, so it cannot route by path
L4 is needed to terminate TLS

rationaleConflicts.r3: TLS termination here is L7 work; an L4 balancer passes the encrypted bytes through.

questions.explanation: Path routing requires reading HTTP, which means L7.

questions.prompt: Health checks run every 5 s and a backend is removed after 3 failures. It serves 100 requests/s when it dies. About how many requests fail before removal?
questions.explanation: Detection takes up to 3 × 5 s = 15 s; 100 requests/s × 15 s = 1,500 failed requests.

flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports.
HTTP paths, headers, cookies.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: What happens to a request at each kind of balancer
steps: An L4 balancer receives TCP or UDP packets and picks a backend using the 5-tuple (source IP and port, destination IP and port, protocol). It forwards bytes without reading them, so it is very fast and works for any protocol.
An L7 balancer terminates the connection (usually including TLS), parses the HTTP request, and routes on host, path, headers or cookies, for example /api/payments to the payments pool.
Because it understands HTTP, an L7 balancer can retry idempotent requests on another backend, add headers, compress responses, enforce rate limits and run a web application firewall.

Health checks run continuously: every few seconds the balancer calls each backend (a TCP connect for L4, an HTTP GET /healthz for L7). After a set number of consecutive failures it marks the backend unhealthy and stops sending traffic; after a set number of successes it adds it back.

Good health endpoints check the process can serve (it can reach its own dependencies within a timeout) but avoid failing just because a shared downstream is down, otherwise every backend fails together.
When removing a backend for a deploy, the balancer drains connections: no new requests, but in-flight ones finish within a timeout.

useWhen: L4: very high throughput, non-HTTP protocols (databases, MQTT, game servers), or as the first tier in front of L7 balancers.
L7: path- or host-based routing, canary releases by header, auth and rate limiting at the edge, gRPC routing per method.
avoidWhen: Do not put content-based routing on an L4 balancer; it cannot see the path.
Do not make health checks deep and strict (checking every downstream): a single shared dependency failure then marks every server unhealthy at once.

rows: HTTP host, path, headers, cookies, body
Routing, retries, WAF, rate limits, canaries

numbers.title: How many requests fail before a dead server is removed?
assumptions: 10 backends sharing 1,000 requests per second evenly
Health check every 5 s; 3 consecutive failures mark a backend unhealthy
steps: Each backend gets 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 requests per second.
Detection takes up to 3 checks × 5 s = 15 s.
Failed requests ≈ 100 × 15 = 1,500 in that window.
With a 2 s interval and 2 failures to trip: 2 × 2 = 4 s, so about 100 × 4 = 400 failures; with passive health checks (eject after a few real errors) it can be under a second.
numbers.result: Aggressive health checks plus passive outlier detection and safe retries cut the damage from about 1,500 failed requests to a few hundred or fewer.

india.title: Routing a payments app by path
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: Consider a payments app in India with very different traffic types behind one domain: /api/upi/collect for payment requests, /api/bills for bill payments, and /static for app assets. An L7 balancer can send each path to its own pool, so a surge in bill payments on the first of the month does not starve UPI payment requests, and it can give the payment path stricter timeouts and no automatic retries (to avoid double debits) while retrying idempotent reads. In front of the L7 tier, an L4 balancer spreads raw TCP connections across many L7 instances at very low cost. Health checks on the UPI pool should test the service's own readiness, not the bank's availability, so one slow bank does not take every server out of rotation.

pitfalls.trap: 'The load balancer will retry failed requests' for every endpoint.
pitfalls.say: 'Retries only for idempotent requests or ones carrying an idempotency key; a payment POST must not be blindly retried.'

pitfalls.trap: Health checks that test every downstream dependency.
pitfalls.say: 'Liveness checks the process; readiness checks it can serve. A shared downstream outage is handled by circuit breakers, not by failing every health check.'

deep.diagram:
clients -> [L4 LB]  (TCP, fast)
              |-> [L7 LB 1] --/api/upi-->   [UPI pool]
              '-> [L7 LB 2] --/api/bills--> [bills pool]
                            --/static-->    [CDN/origin]
takeaways: L4 balancers forward connections by IP and port; L7 balancers route by HTTP content.
L7 enables path routing, retries, canaries, WAF and rate limits at some CPU cost.
Detection time = check interval × failure threshold; shorten it and add passive checks.
Keep health checks shallow and drain connections during deploys.

title: Forward vs Reverse Proxy
objectives: A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Nginx/Envoy as a reverse proxy hides backends, terminates TLS, compresses and caches. A forward proxy (corporate) sits in front of clients to filter or anonymise outbound traffic.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client” to “Response”, via “Reverse proxy”.
steps: Client
Reverse proxy
TLS + gzip + cache
Upstream app
Response

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Mixing up the two. Reverse = server side; forward = client side.

questions.prompt: A company filters which websites employees can visit. What sits in the path?
questions.explanation: Forward proxies act for clients on outbound traffic.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical reverse-proxy job?

choices.label: Terminate TLS and compress responses for the app servers
Cache public websites for a school network
Hide employees’ IP addresses from websites
Filter which websites employees may visit

questions.explanation: The other three act on the client side, which is forward-proxy work.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy sits in front of what?

choices.label: Your users’ devices, facing outgoing traffic
Your servers, facing incoming client traffic

questions.explanation: Reverse proxies represent servers; forward proxies represent clients.

questions.prompt: Order a request through a reverse proxy.
questions.explanation: The proxy handles cross-cutting work before the app sees the request.

questions.prompt: Static CSS and images are 70% of requests, the proxy does no caching, and app servers sit at 90% CPU. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Let the reverse proxy cache or serve static files so the app only handles dynamic requests.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy caches 80% of 20,000 requests/s. How many requests per second still reach the origin?
questions.explanation: 20,000 × 0.8 = 16,000 are served from cache, so 20,000 − 16,000 = 4,000 reach the origin.

flashcards.front: Reverse proxy sits in front of?
flashcards.back: Servers.

flashcards.front: Forward proxy sits in front of?
flashcards.back: Clients.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Same middle box, opposite sides
steps: A forward proxy sits on the client side. Clients are configured to send requests to it, and it fetches from the internet on their behalf. Servers see the proxy's IP, not the client's.
Organisations use forward proxies to enforce outbound policy (block sites, scan downloads), to log access, and to share a cache of common downloads.
A reverse proxy sits on the server side. Clients think they are talking to the website; the proxy receives the request and forwards it to one of many hidden backends.
The reverse proxy terminates TLS, load balances, caches responses, compresses them, enforces rate limits and hides the backend topology. Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy and CDNs are typical examples.
It passes the real client IP to the backend in a header such as X-Forwarded-For, which the backend must trust only from the proxy.
A CDN is a globally distributed reverse proxy with caches close to users; an API gateway is a reverse proxy specialised for APIs (auth, quotas, routing).

useWhen: Reverse proxy: in front of every web service, for TLS, routing, caching, compression and protection.
Forward proxy: corporate or school networks controlling outbound access, or services that must reach the internet from a fixed egress IP (some partner APIs allow-list IPs).
avoidWhen: Do not add another reverse-proxy hop inside the cluster unless it does real work; each hop adds latency and a failure point.
Do not trust X-Forwarded-For from arbitrary clients; it is easily forged.

rows: TLS, load balancing, caching, WAF, rate limits

numbers.title: What a caching reverse proxy saves the origin
assumptions: 20,000 requests per second for product pages at peak
80% of them are cacheable for 60 s at the proxy
Each origin render costs about 20 ms of CPU
steps: Requests served from the proxy cache = 20,000 × 0.8 = 16,000 per second.
Requests reaching the origin = 20,000 − 16,000 = 4,000 per second.
Origin CPU needed = 4,000 × 0.02 s = 80 CPU-seconds per second, about 80 cores, versus 20,000 × 0.02 = 400 cores without the cache.
That is a 5× reduction in origin capacity.
numbers.result: An 80% cache hit rate at the reverse proxy cuts origin load by 5× (from about 400 cores to about 80).

india.title: Sale-day product pages behind reverse proxies
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During an Indian e-commerce sale, millions of shoppers hit the same few hundred deal pages in the first minutes. Rendering each page from scratch at the origin would need several times more servers, as the maths above shows. Retailers put CDNs and caching reverse proxies in front: the shared parts of a page (product details, images) are cached for seconds to minutes, while price and stock are fetched separately and kept fresh. Many corporate networks in India, meanwhile, run forward proxies for employees: outbound traffic goes through a proxy that blocks some categories of sites and logs access. Same kind of software, opposite side of the connection.

pitfalls.trap: Mixing up forward and reverse proxies.
pitfalls.say: 'A forward proxy represents clients going out; a reverse proxy represents servers taking requests in.'

pitfalls.trap: Caching personalised responses at a shared proxy.
pitfalls.say: 'Only cache responses that are the same for everyone, or vary the cache key by the relevant header; user-specific data needs Cache-Control: private.'

deep.diagram:
Forward:  [employee PCs] -> [forward proxy] -> internet sites
Reverse:  internet users -> [reverse proxy / CDN] -> [app 1..N]
takeaways: Forward proxies act for clients; reverse proxies act for servers.
Reverse proxies do TLS, load balancing, caching, compression and protection.
CDNs and API gateways are specialised reverse proxies.
Never cache personalised data in a shared proxy, and trust forwarded-IP headers only from your own proxy.

title: Stateless Services & Sessions
objectives: Explain what makes a service stateless
Decide where session state should live
Weigh sticky sessions against a shared session store

cards.title: What stateless means
cards.body: A stateless service keeps nothing about a user in its own memory between requests. Any instance can serve any request, so the balancer spreads load freely and an instance can die without logging anyone out.

cards.title: Where session state goes
cards.body: Move it out: a shared store such as Redis keyed by session id, or a signed token the client sends each time. The database stays the source of truth for durable data.

cards.title: Sticky sessions
cards.body: Sticky sessions pin a user to one instance with a cookie. It is a quick fix for a stateful app, but load spreads unevenly and the session dies with the instance.

cards.title: A request with external sessions
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client sends a cookie with the session id” to “Changes are written back to Redis”, via “Balancer picks any healthy instance”.
steps: Client sends a cookie with the session id
Balancer picks any healthy instance
Instance loads the session from Redis
Instance handles the request
Changes are written back to Redis

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Keeping a shopping cart in server memory and then scaling out. Users bounce between instances and their carts vanish. Move the cart to a shared store first.

questions.prompt: After adding a second app server, users randomly lose their carts. Most likely cause?

choices.label: The database cannot handle two servers
Carts live in each server’s memory and requests bounce between servers
Round robin sends all traffic to one server

questions.explanation: In-memory state breaks as soon as requests can land on different instances.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of sticky sessions?

choices.label: They add a full round trip to every request
They stop the balancer from health checking
Uneven load, and a session is lost when its instance dies
They require a JWT on every request

questions.explanation: Pinning users ties their state to one machine.

questions.prompt: Where should session state live for a horizontally scaled web app?

choices.label: In each instance’s memory, with sticky sessions turned off
In files on each server’s local disk
In a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed token the client sends

questions.explanation: Shared or client-held state lets any instance serve any request.

questions.prompt: Order a request that uses an external session store.

items.label: Instance loads the session from Redis

questions.explanation: The instance holds nothing between requests.

questions.prompt: Choose a session approach for a 20-instance checkout service where sessions must survive deploys.

approaches.label: Sticky sessions
approaches.description: Pin each user to one instance

rationaleOptions.label: Sticky sessions spread load evenly
Sessions survive an instance restart during a deploy
Any instance can serve any request

rationaleConflicts.r3: Pinning users makes load uneven as busy sessions pile up on some instances.

questions.explanation: An external store keeps instances disposable.

questions.prompt: 10 million sessions of about 1 KB each are stored in Redis with one replica. Roughly how much memory is that in total?
questions.explanation: 10 million sessions at 1 KB each is about 10 GB; a primary plus one replica doubles that to about 20 GB.

flashcards.front: After adding a second app server, users randomly lose their carts. Most likely cause?
flashcards.back: Carts live in each server’s memory and requests bounce between servers. In-memory state breaks as soon as requests can land on different instances.

flashcards.front: What is the main downside of sticky sessions?
flashcards.back: Uneven load, and a session is lost when its instance dies. Pinning users ties their state to one machine.

flashcards.front: Where should session state live for a horizontally scaled web app?
flashcards.back: In a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed token the client sends. Shared or client-held state lets any instance serve any request.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Moving state out of the web server
steps: A stateful server keeps the user's session (login, cart, wizard progress) in its own memory. The next request must reach the same server, and a restart logs everyone out.
Sticky sessions patch this at the load balancer by pinning each user to one server (by cookie or IP hash). Load can become uneven, and a server failure still loses its sessions.
A stateless server keeps nothing between requests. Each request carries a session ID cookie, and the server looks the session up in a shared store such as Redis.
Alternatively, the session itself can travel in a signed token (a JWT): the server verifies the signature and reads the claims without a lookup, at the cost of harder revocation.
Files and uploads go to object storage, not local disk; caches are either shared or treated as disposable.
Now any server can handle any request, so you can add, remove or replace servers freely and the load balancer can use any algorithm.

useWhen: Stateless services with a session store: almost every web and API tier that needs to autoscale or survive server loss.
Signed tokens: when you want to avoid a session lookup on every request and can live with short expiries plus a revocation strategy.
Sticky sessions: legacy apps you cannot change yet, or WebSocket connections that are naturally pinned.
avoidWhen: Avoid in-memory sessions on autoscaled servers; scale-in events log users out.
Avoid long-lived JWTs for things that must be revocable instantly (bank logouts, banned users) unless you also keep a denylist.

rows: One fast lookup (sub-millisecond in the same zone)
Hard: wait for expiry or keep a denylist

numbers.title: Sizing a Redis session store
assumptions: About 1 KB per session (user ID, roles, cart pointer, CSRF token)
50,000 requests per second, each reading its session
steps: Memory = 10M sessions × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB, so about 20 GB with one replica.
Lookups = 50,000 per second; one Redis node can serve well over 100,000 simple GETs per second, so a single primary covers it with headroom.
Shard by session ID across 2–3 primaries anyway, to keep each node's memory small and limit the blast radius.
Added latency per request ≈ one round trip inside the zone, typically well under 1 ms.
numbers.result: About 10 GB of data (20 GB with replicas), 50K reads/s and sub-millisecond lookups: a small Redis cluster buys a fully stateless web tier.

india.title: IRCTC-style booking when servers come and go
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: In a train booking flow during Tatkal, a user moves through search, seat selection, passenger details and payment within a few minutes, while the platform adds servers to absorb the 10:00 spike. If the booking wizard's progress lived in one server's memory, any scale-in, crash or deploy would throw users back to the start at the worst possible moment. Keeping the session and the in-progress booking in a shared store keyed by session ID means any server can serve the next step, and a server can be killed without users noticing. The seat hold itself lives in the inventory database with an expiry, not in the session, because it must be consistent across all users.

pitfalls.trap: Scaling out while sessions live in server memory.
pitfalls.say: 'First make the tier stateless: sessions in Redis, files in object storage; then autoscale behind any balancing algorithm.'

pitfalls.trap: Choosing JWTs without a revocation plan.
pitfalls.say: 'Short-lived access tokens, say 15 minutes, plus refresh tokens I can revoke server-side.'

deep.diagram:
[LB] -> [web 1] --+
     -> [web 2] --+--> [Redis: session:abc -> {user 7, cart 91}]
     -> [web 3] --+--> [object storage: uploads]
takeaways: Stateless servers let you scale out, replace and deploy freely.
Keep sessions in a shared store or a signed token, not in server memory.
Sticky sessions are a stopgap: uneven load and lost sessions on failure.
Signed tokens remove lookups but make revocation hard; keep them short-lived.

title: Where to Cache
objectives: Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Reads often follow a power law: a small set of keys gets most traffic. Serving them from memory (Redis, local LRU) drops latency from ms to µs and shields the DB.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 7 steps from “Request” to “Populate cache”, via “Check cache”.
steps: Request
Check cache
Hit
return
Miss
DB
Populate cache

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Caching everything blindly. Cache data that is read-heavy and tolerant of brief staleness.

cards.title: Cache layers
cards.body: From the user inward: browser cache, CDN edge, reverse proxy, an in-process cache in each app instance, a shared cache such as Redis, then the database’s own buffer pool. The closer to the user, the faster the hit and the harder it is to invalidate.

questions.prompt: What does a 95% cache hit rate mean?

choices.label: The cache holds 95% of the database
95 of every 100 reads are served from cache; 5 go to the database

questions.explanation: Hit rate is about reads served, not data stored.

questions.prompt: 20,000 reads/s with a 90% hit rate. How many reads/s reach the database?
Which data is the best cache candidate?

choices.label: Click logs written constantly and read once by a batch job
Product pages read thousands of times per update
A wallet balance during a transfer

questions.explanation: Cache read-heavy data that tolerates brief staleness.

questions.prompt: Fifty app instances each keep an in-process cache instead of sharing Redis. Main downside?

choices.label: Each instance then needs its own database
Each instance has its own copy, so a change must be invalidated in all 50
In-process memory is slower than a network call to Redis

questions.explanation: Local caches are the fastest hit but the hardest to keep consistent.

questions.prompt: Order a cache-aside read.

items.label: Store the result in the cache

questions.explanation: On a hit the flow stops at the cache.

questions.prompt: 100,000 reads/s hit a cache. If the hit rate rises from 90% to 99%, what happens to database reads?
questions.explanation: Database reads are the misses: 10% of 100,000 = 10,000/s, then 1% of 100,000 = 1,000/s, a 10× drop.

flashcards.back: hits ÷ (hits + misses).
Read-heavy, hot, staleness-tolerant data.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: The layers a read can be answered from, nearest first
steps: Client cache: the browser or app keeps responses according to Cache-Control and ETag headers. A hit costs no network at all.
CDN edge: a point of presence near the user caches static files and cacheable API responses. A hit costs one short round trip.
Reverse proxy or API gateway cache: shared responses cached in the data centre, in front of the app servers.
Application cache: an in-process map (fastest, but per server and lost on restart) or a shared cache such as Redis or Memcached (one network hop, shared by all servers).
Database buffer pool: the database keeps hot pages in RAM, so even a 'database read' is often a memory read.
On a miss at every layer, the read goes to disk or to another service, and the result is stored on the way back so the next read is a hit.

useWhen: Read-heavy data that changes rarely relative to how often it is read: product details, profiles, configuration, rendered pages.
Expensive results: aggregated counts, search results, recommendations, anything that takes many queries to build.
Static assets: images, scripts, video segments, always at the CDN.
avoidWhen: Data that must be exact on every read, such as an account balance used to approve a payment or seats left at the moment of booking; read it from the source of truth.
Write-heavy data that is rarely re-read: you pay to fill and invalidate a cache nobody hits.

rows: Hard: headers and versioned URLs only

numbers.title: Why the last few percent of hit rate matter
assumptions: Cache hit costs 1 ms, database read costs 10 ms
steps: Average latency = hit rate × 1 ms + miss rate × 10 ms.
At 90% hits: 0.9 of reads cost 1 ms and 0.1 cost 10 ms, so 0.9 + 1.0 ≈ 1.9 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.1 = 10,000 per second.
At 99% hits: 0.99 + 0.1 ≈ 1.09 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.01 = 1,000 per second.
Going from 90% to 99% cuts database load 10×, even though the hit rate only rose 9 points.
numbers.result: Database load is driven by the miss rate: 10% misses means 10,000 DB reads/s, 1% means 1,000. Quote miss rate, not just hit rate, when sizing the database.

india.title: Cricket score widgets during a big match
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During a high-profile India match, tens of millions of people may refresh scores in news apps, streaming apps and search results. The score itself changes at most once a ball, roughly every 30–40 seconds, and is the same for everyone. So it is cached at every layer: the app keeps the last score, the CDN caches the score API response for a few seconds, and the origin reads from an in-memory cache fed by the scoring service. If 10 million clients each poll every 10 seconds, that is 1 million requests per second; with a 5-second CDN TTL, each of a few hundred edge locations refreshes about once every 5 seconds, so the origin sees on the order of a hundred requests per second or less (fewer still behind an origin shield).

pitfalls.trap: 'Add Redis' without saying what is cached or for how long.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd cache restaurant menus by restaurant ID for 5 minutes with explicit invalidation on menu edits; prices at checkout come from the database.'

pitfalls.trap: Caching data that must be strongly consistent.
pitfalls.say: 'Wallet balances are read from the primary at payment time; the cached balance is only for display.'

deep.diagram:
app cache -> CDN edge -> gateway cache -> app (in-process) -> Redis -> DB buffer pool -> disk
  fastest, least shared  ------------------------------------------>  slowest, source of truth
takeaways: Cache at the layer nearest the user that can still be invalidated correctly.
Database load follows the miss rate: 99% hits means one-tenth the load of 90%.
Cache what is read often, changes rarely and is expensive to build.
Never approve money or inventory from a cache.

title: Cache Strategies
objectives: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and sets cache. Write-through: write cache and DB synchronously (fresh, slower writes). Write-behind: write cache, flush DB later (fast, risk of loss).

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Read cache” to “Return”, via “Miss”.
steps: Read cache
Miss
Read DB
Set cache with TTL
Return

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using write-behind for payments. Losing buffered writes on a crash is unacceptable for money.

questions.prompt: Which strategy can lose writes if the cache node crashes?
questions.explanation: Write-behind acknowledges before the database has the data.

questions.prompt: What does write-through give you, and at what cost?

choices.label: Fast writes, but data can be lost on a crash
Cache and database are updated together, so reads are fresh; writes are slower
No cache misses ever, at no cost

questions.explanation: Both stores are written synchronously.

questions.prompt: Order a cache-aside read on a miss.

items.label: Set the cache with a TTL

questions.explanation: The application, not the cache, loads data on a miss.

questions.prompt: Pick a caching strategy for a product catalogue.
constraints: A few seconds of staleness is fine

approaches.label: Cache-aside with a TTL
approaches.description: Load on miss, expire after a while

rationaleOptions.label: A TTL bounds staleness after an update
Write-behind is needed to keep reads fresh
Only items people actually view end up cached

rationaleConflicts.r3: Write-behind speeds up writes and risks losing them; it does nothing for read freshness.

questions.explanation: Read-heavy and staleness-tolerant is the classic cache-aside case.

questions.prompt: Why not use write-behind for a payment ledger?

choices.label: It forces every read to go to the database
Payment data cannot be stored in Redis
Buffered writes can be lost in a crash, and losing money records is unacceptable

questions.explanation: Durability matters more than write speed for money.

questions.prompt: A like counter takes 20,000 likes/s and flushes from cache to the DB every 5 s. If the cache dies just before a flush, how many likes could be lost?

choices.label: None; the database already has them

questions.explanation: Five seconds of unflushed writes: 5 × 20,000 = 100,000 likes.

flashcards.back: Cache-aside (lazy loading).
Losing unflushed writes.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How the cache and the database stay in step under each strategy
steps: Cache-aside (lazy loading), read path: the app checks the cache; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns it.
Cache-aside, write path: the app writes to the database, then deletes the cache key (rather than updating it) so the next read reloads fresh data.
Write-through: every write goes to the cache and the database together, and the write succeeds only when both do. Reads after writes are always warm and fresh.

Write-behind (write-back): writes go to the cache and are acknowledged immediately; the cache flushes them to the database later in batches. Very fast writes, but a cache crash before the flush loses data.
Read-through: the cache itself loads from the database on a miss (the app only talks to the cache). It behaves like cache-aside but the loading logic lives in the cache layer.
Whatever the strategy, give keys a TTL as a safety net so any missed invalidation heals itself.

useWhen: Cache-aside: the default for read-heavy services; only requested data is cached and the cache can fail without losing data.
Write-through: data that is read soon after being written and must be fresh, such as a user profile right after editing.
Write-behind: high-volume counters and metrics (likes, views) where losing a few seconds of increments is acceptable.
avoidWhen: Write-behind for money, orders or anything that must not be lost.
Write-through for data that is rarely read: every write pays for a cache entry nobody uses.

rows: Yes, if the cache dies before flushing

numbers.title: What write-behind buys and risks for a like counter
assumptions: Flush to the database every 5 seconds, batched per post
On average a hot post receives many likes per window, so each batch row covers many likes
steps: Direct writes: 20,000 database updates per second.
With write-behind, each flush writes one row per post touched; if 2,000 distinct posts are liked per 5-second window, that is 2,000 updates per flush ÷ 5 s = 400 updates per second.
Write reduction ≈ 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50×.
Risk: if the cache node dies just before a flush, up to 5 s × 20,000 = 100,000 likes are lost.
numbers.result: Write-behind turns about 20,000 writes/s into about 400, at the risk of losing up to about 100,000 likes in a crash. Fine for likes, never for payments.

india.title: Restaurant menus versus wallet balances
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: A food delivery platform in India reads restaurant menus far more often than restaurants edit them, so menus suit cache-aside: read from Redis, on a miss load from the database, and when a restaurant edits its menu, write the database and delete the cache key. A short TTL, say 5 minutes, heals any missed delete. A digital wallet balance is the opposite case. When a user pays, the debit must happen in the database inside a transaction, and the balance used to approve the payment must come from the source of truth. A cached balance can be shown on the home screen, refreshed after each transaction, but write-behind would be unacceptable because a cache crash could lose money movements.

pitfalls.trap: Updating the cache value on write instead of deleting it.
pitfalls.say: 'I write the database, then delete the key. Concurrent writers can otherwise leave an older value in the cache.'

pitfalls.trap: Proposing write-behind for orders or payments.
pitfalls.say: 'Write-behind can lose acknowledged writes, so I'd only use it for counters; orders are written to the database first.'

deep.diagram:
cache-aside read:  app -> cache? hit -> return
                          miss -> DB -> set cache(TTL) -> return
cache-aside write: app -> DB -> delete cache key
write-behind:      app -> cache (ack) ... batch flush -> DB
takeaways: Cache-aside is the safe default: read through on miss, delete the key on write, always set a TTL.
Write-through keeps reads fresh at the cost of slower writes.
Write-behind gives fast writes but can lose data; use it only where loss is tolerable.
Prefer deleting keys over updating them to avoid races.

title: Eviction Policies
objectives: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: LRU evicts least recently used — good default. LFU keeps frequently used items — good for stable hot sets. TTL expires data by age regardless of use.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Cache full” to “Insert new key”, via “New key arrives”.
steps: Cache full
New key arrives
Pick victim by policy
Evict
Insert new key

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Never setting TTLs, so stale entries live forever after the source changes.

questions.prompt: Which policy evicts the item not accessed for the longest time?
questions.explanation: Least recently used.

questions.prompt: A stable set of popular products gets most traffic, but a nightly job reads every product once. Which policy best keeps the popular set cached?

choices.label: FIFO, because it ignores access patterns
LFU, because one read does not make an item frequent
LRU, because the scanned items were used most recently
No policy: a full cache stops accepting keys

questions.explanation: Under LRU the scan pushes out the hot set; LFU keeps items that are used often.

questions.prompt: A price changed in the database, but the cache served the old price for days. What was missing?

choices.label: A TTL (or explicit invalidation) on the cached price

questions.explanation: Eviction only happens under memory pressure; TTLs bound staleness.

questions.prompt: What does FIFO evict?

choices.label: The item inserted earliest, regardless of how often it is used

questions.explanation: FIFO ignores access entirely.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a full cache gets a new key.
questions.explanation: The policy only decides which key leaves.

questions.prompt: A catalogue has 10 million items of 2 KB each, and 20% of items get 90% of views. About how much memory caches the hot set?
questions.explanation: Hot set = 20% of 10 million = 2 million items × 2 KB ≈ 4 GB.

flashcards.back: Hash map + doubly linked list.
Stable, skewed hot sets.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: What happens when the cache is full and a new key arrives
steps: Every cache has a memory limit. When a write would exceed it, the cache must evict something first.
LRU (least recently used) evicts the key not read for the longest time. A hash map plus a doubly linked list makes both lookup and 'move to front' O(1).
LFU (least frequently used) evicts the key with the fewest accesses, usually with counters that decay over time so yesterday's popular keys can still be evicted.
FIFO evicts the oldest inserted key regardless of use: simple, but it will evict a hot key just because it is old.
TTL expiry removes keys when their time is up, independent of memory pressure. It bounds staleness rather than size.
Production caches approximate: Redis samples a few keys (5 by default) and evicts the best candidate among them, which is close to true LRU or LFU at a fraction of the bookkeeping.

useWhen: LRU: general-purpose caches where recently used data is likely to be used again (sessions, pages, profiles).
LFU: steady popularity patterns where a one-off scan should not push out long-term favourites (product catalogue, popular videos).
TTL: anything that must not be served stale beyond a bound, layered on top of LRU or LFU.
avoidWhen: Plain LRU when big sequential scans (a nightly export) pass through the cache; they flush the hot set. LFU or scan-resistant variants handle that better.
FIFO for skewed workloads; it ignores popularity completely.

rows: One big scan evicts the hot set
Does not bound memory by itself

numbers.title: How big must the cache be for a 90% hit rate?
assumptions: 10 million products, about 2 KB of cached data each
Popularity is heavily skewed: about 20% of products receive about 90% of views (an illustrative skew; measure yours)
steps: Memory for the hot set = 2,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 4 GB.
Caching everything would need 10,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 20 GB.
With LRU or LFU and about 4–5 GB, the cache holds the hot set and reaches roughly 90% hits; the last 10% of hits would cost the other 16 GB.
numbers.result: About 4 GB buys roughly 90% hits under this skew; going further costs memory much faster than it adds hits. Size the cache for the hot set, then let the eviction policy keep it hot.

india.title: A video catalogue during a festival release
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Take a video streaming catalogue in India. On a normal day the popular shows stay popular for weeks, which suits LFU with decay: an occasional one-off visit to an old title should not evict a show watched by millions. On a festival weekend, though, a big new release appears and is watched heavily within hours. Pure LFU would be slow to keep it, because its count starts at zero; LRU would keep it at once. Redis offers both (allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu), and LFU's counters decay so new hits catch up quickly. Many teams measure hit rate under both policies on a replay of real traffic before choosing.

pitfalls.trap: 'Use LRU' with no thought about the access pattern.
pitfalls.say: 'Popularity is stable and skewed, so LFU with decay; if a nightly batch scans the catalogue, I'd keep it from polluting the cache.'

pitfalls.trap: Confusing TTL with eviction.
pitfalls.say: 'TTL bounds staleness; the eviction policy decides what goes when memory is full. I'd set both.'

deep.diagram:
LRU list (most recent first):  [P9] [P2] [P7] [P1]  <- evict P1
read P7  ->                     [P7] [P9] [P2] [P1]
insert P5 (full) ->             [P5] [P7] [P9] [P2]   (P1 evicted)
takeaways: LRU evicts the least recently used key; LFU the least frequently used; FIFO the oldest inserted.
TTL bounds staleness, not memory; use it together with an eviction policy.
Size the cache for the hot set; skew means a small cache can give a high hit rate.
Real caches approximate LRU and LFU by sampling.

title: Stampede/Penetration/Avalanche
objectives: Protect against many simultaneous misses and single overloaded keys.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB. Fix with request coalescing (single flight), locks, early refresh, and TTL jitter. Hot keys: replicate or add local caches.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Protect against many simultaneous misses and single overloaded keys.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Hot key expires” to “All waiters served”, via “Many misses”.
steps: Hot key expires
Many misses
Single-flight lock
One DB read
All waiters served

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Setting identical TTLs on a million keys, so they all expire together.

cards.title: Penetration and avalanche
cards.body: Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist (often bots) miss the cache every time and hit the database; cache the “not found” briefly or check a Bloom filter. Avalanche: many keys expire together, or a cache node dies, and the database takes the full load; add TTL jitter and replicate the cache.

questions.prompt: Thousands of requests miss the same just-expired key at once. Best fix?

choices.label: Lower the TTL so the key refreshes more often
Let one request rebuild the key while the others wait (single flight)
Add database replicas and nothing else

questions.explanation: Coalescing turns thousands of identical misses into one database read.

questions.prompt: Bots request random product ids that do not exist; every request misses and hits the database. Fix?

choices.label: Switch eviction from LRU to LFU
Raise the TTL of existing keys
Cache the “not found” result briefly, or check a Bloom filter first

questions.explanation: The cache never holds keys that do not exist unless you store the negative answer.

questions.prompt: A million keys were loaded at 9:00 with a one-hour TTL. At 10:00 the database falls over. Fix?

choices.label: Add random jitter to TTLs so expiries spread out
Set every TTL to exactly two hours
Use single flight per key, nothing else

questions.explanation: Identical TTLs make keys expire together; jitter spreads them.

questions.prompt: Order single-flight handling of a hot key.
questions.explanation: Only the lock holder goes to the database.

questions.prompt: The live-score key expires and 50K requests/s miss together. Click where it breaks.
questions.explanation: The database takes every miss at once. Coalescing or early refresh protects it.

questions.prompt: A hot key read 50,000 times/s expires and takes 200 ms to rebuild. Without coalescing, roughly how many duplicate rebuilds can hit the DB?
questions.explanation: 50,000 requests/s × 0.2 s = 10,000 requests arrive while the key is missing, each of which could trigger a rebuild.

flashcards.back: Many concurrent misses for one key overwhelm the DB.
Replicate key, local cache, or split key.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Three ways a cache fails under load, and the fix for each
steps: Stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires, and thousands of concurrent requests all miss at once and all query the database for the same value.

Fix the stampede with request coalescing: the first miss takes a short lock (or a single-flight promise) and rebuilds the value; the others wait briefly or serve the stale value. Probabilistic early refresh rebuilds a hot key shortly before it expires.

Avalanche: many keys expire at the same moment (for example everything loaded at startup with the same 1-hour TTL), or the whole cache cluster restarts, so the database suddenly takes all the traffic.
Fix the avalanche with TTL jitter (for example 60 minutes ± 10%), staggered warm-up, a replicated cache that survives node loss, and rate limiting or circuit breakers in front of the database.
Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist (often from bots or bugs) always miss the cache and always hit the database.
Fix penetration by caching 'not found' results with a short TTL, validating IDs early, and putting a Bloom filter of existing IDs in front of the database.

useWhen: Coalescing and early refresh: any hot key with expensive rebuilds (home page feed, trending list, sale banners).
Jitter: every time you set TTLs in bulk.
Negative caching and Bloom filters: public endpoints where IDs are guessable or enumerable.
avoidWhen: Do not hold a rebuild lock without a timeout; if the rebuilder dies, everyone waits.
Do not cache 'not found' for long on data that is about to be created (a just-placed order), or users will not see their own new item.

rows: Single-flight lock, serve stale, early refresh
Many keys expire together or cache restarts
TTL jitter, warm-up, replicas, DB protection
Memory for filter; brief false 'not found' risk

numbers.title: A stampede on one hot key
assumptions: A trending-deals key is read 50,000 times per second
Rebuilding it takes 200 ms of database queries
The key expires with no protection
steps: Requests arriving during the 200 ms rebuild window = 50,000 × 0.2 = 10,000.
Without coalescing, up to 10,000 identical rebuild queries hit the database at once.
With single-flight, 1 request rebuilds and the other 9,999 wait or get the stale value.
Database queries per expiry fall from about 10,000 to 1.
numbers.result: One unprotected hot key can send about 10,000 identical queries to the database in 200 ms; coalescing makes it one.

india.title: Sale-day banners and the 'deal of the hour'
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Indian e-commerce sales often feature hourly deals that open at a fixed minute, say 'deal of the hour' at 12:00. Every shopper's app requests the same deal list at that minute, and if the cached list was given a TTL ending exactly at 12:00, the expiry and the traffic spike coincide: a textbook stampede on one key. The safer design prepares the next hour's list in advance and swaps it into the cache before 12:00, uses single-flight rebuilds in case of a miss, and adds TTL jitter to everything loaded in bulk. Bots requesting random product IDs to find unlisted deals are a penetration risk, handled with negative caching, ID validation and rate limiting.

pitfalls.trap: Treating all three problems as 'add more cache'.
pitfalls.say: 'Stampede is one hot key: coalesce. Avalanche is mass expiry: jitter and warm-up. Penetration is missing keys: negative cache and a Bloom filter.'

pitfalls.trap: Using a lock without a timeout or a stale fallback.
pitfalls.say: 'The rebuild lock has a short timeout, and waiting readers fall back to the stale value if it's not ready.'

deep.diagram:
t=0  key 'deals' expires
     50K req/s --miss--> [single-flight]
                           |-> 1 rebuild -> DB
                           '-> others: serve stale / wait 50 ms
takeaways: Stampede: many misses on one hot key; fix with coalescing, stale-while-revalidate or early refresh.
Avalanche: many keys expiring together or a cache restart; fix with jitter, warm-up and replicas.
Penetration: lookups for keys that don't exist; fix with negative caching and Bloom filters.
Always protect the database behind the cache with limits.

mechanism.title: How a CDN serves a file
steps: DNS (or anycast routing) sends the user to a nearby CDN point of presence (PoP).
The edge server checks its cache for the URL. On a hit it returns the file immediately, typically within a few tens of milliseconds.
On a miss, it fetches from a regional tier or an origin shield (one designated cache in front of the origin), which in turn fetches from the origin only if it also misses.
The response is cached at the edge for as long as Cache-Control allows (max-age / s-maxage), and later requests for that URL are served locally.
For changes, give each version of a file a new URL (app.3f9c2a.js) so you can cache it for a year and still ship updates instantly; purge only for mistakes.
For private content, the app issues signed URLs or signed cookies with an expiry; the edge checks the signature, so it can serve paid video without calling your servers.

useWhen: Static assets: images, scripts, stylesheets, fonts, app bundles.
Video: segments for HLS and DASH streaming, which are ideal cache objects.
Cacheable API responses that are the same for many users for a few seconds (scores, prices on listing pages, configuration).
avoidWhen: Personalised or authenticated responses without careful cache keys; a shared cache can leak one user's data to another.
Data that must be exact per request (checkout totals, seat availability at booking).

rows: Versioned URLs (content hash in the name)
None; old files simply age out
Seconds to minutes across all PoPs
Easy to forget a URL; a purge storm hits the origin

numbers.title: Egress for a live stream with and without a CDN
assumptions: Average bitrate 2 Mbit/s (a mix of mobile qualities)
Video split into 6-second segments; each edge fetches each segment from the shield once
steps: Total delivery bandwidth = 10,000,000 × 2 Mbit/s = 20,000,000 Mbit/s = 20 Tbit/s, all served by CDN edges.
Without a CDN, the origin itself would have to push about 20 Tbit/s.
With a CDN, each edge fetches each segment about once per rendition, so the origin or shield serves roughly 500 edges × a handful of renditions per segment.
Origin egress ≈ 500 × 2 Mbit/s × 5 renditions = 5,000 Mbit/s = 5 Gbit/s, about 4,000× less than 20 Tbit/s.
numbers.result: The CDN carries about 20 Tbit/s at the edges while the origin sends a few Gbit/s. Live streaming at this scale is only possible because each edge fetches each segment once.

india.title: Live cricket at record concurrency
india.label: Publicly reported concurrency; bandwidth is an illustrative estimate
india.body: Indian streaming services have publicly reported record live audiences for cricket: Disney+ Hotstar reported about 25.3 million concurrent viewers during the 2019 World Cup semi-final between India and New Zealand, and later reported higher peaks for subsequent tournaments. At an illustrative average of 2 Mbit/s per viewer, 25 million viewers need about 50 Tbit/s of delivery capacity, far beyond any single origin. That load is spread across CDN PoPs, including caches placed inside Indian internet providers' networks, while the origin produces each 6-second segment once per quality level. Capacity is planned and pre-provisioned with CDN partners well before a big match, because autoscaling cannot add terabits in minutes.

pitfalls.trap: Relying on purges to ship new JavaScript.
pitfalls.say: 'Assets get content-hashed file names and a one-year max-age; index.html is short-lived and points at the new hashes.'

pitfalls.trap: Serving paid video from public URLs.
pitfalls.say: 'The app issues short-lived signed URLs or cookies; the edge verifies the signature without calling our servers.'

deep.diagram:
viewers -> [edge PoP Mumbai] --miss--> [origin shield] --miss--> [origin / packager]
viewers -> [edge PoP Delhi ] --hit--> (served locally)
takeaways: A CDN serves from caches near users; the origin is hit only on misses.
Version asset URLs and cache them for a long time; purge only by exception.
Use signed URLs or cookies for private content.
For big live events, the edge carries terabits while the origin sends each segment once per rendition.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: What happens inside Redis when you run a command
steps: Redis keeps all data in RAM and executes commands one at a time on a single main thread, so each command is atomic without locks. Network I/O can use extra threads in newer versions, but command execution stays single-threaded.

Because commands are tiny in-memory operations, a single node typically serves on the order of 100,000+ simple operations per second with sub-millisecond latency, until one slow command (KEYS *, a huge SORT) blocks everyone behind it.

Data structures do the work on the server: strings and counters (INCR), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets, sorted sets (leaderboards, rate-limit windows), streams (append-only logs), plus HyperLogLog and bitmaps.
Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots write the whole dataset periodically; the AOF appends every write and can fsync every second, losing at most about a second of writes on a crash.
Replication is asynchronous: a replica follows the primary's stream of writes. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted, and writes not yet replicated can be lost.

Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16,384 hash slots spread across primaries. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16,384; hash tags like {user:42} keep related keys in one slot so multi-key commands still work.

useWhen: Caches, sessions, rate limiting counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), short-lived locks, lightweight queues and pub/sub.
Anywhere you need atomic operations on small shared state at high throughput: INCR, ZADD, SET with NX and expiry.
avoidWhen: As the only copy of data you cannot lose, given asynchronous replication and memory-bound capacity.
Datasets far larger than RAM, or workloads needing complex queries and joins.

numbers.title: A live leaderboard for a quiz show
assumptions: 5 million players in one sorted set
About 64 bytes per entry including member ID and overhead (an estimate; check with MEMORY USAGE)
200,000 score updates per second at peak
steps: Memory = 5,000,000 × 64 bytes = 320,000,000 bytes ≈ 320 MB, which fits easily on one node.
ZADD and ZRANK are O(log N); log2 of 5 million is about 22, so each operation is a few dozen steps.
200,000 updates per second is above what one node handles comfortably, so split players into shards (for example 4 sorted sets by player ID), giving 50,000 updates per second per shard.
Global top 10 = take the top 10 from each of the 4 shards (40 entries) and merge them.
numbers.result: About 320 MB of memory and O(log N) updates: sorted sets make a 5-million-player leaderboard cheap. Shard by player and merge the per-shard top 10s for the global top 10.

india.title: Fantasy and quiz contests during IPL
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Fantasy sports and live quiz apps in India see huge, synchronised spikes: when a wicket falls in an IPL match, millions of contest scores change at the same moment and players immediately check their rank. A sorted set per contest gives O(log N) score updates and rank lookups, and the whole leaderboard for a large contest fits in a few hundred megabytes. The heavy part is the write burst, so updates are batched per ball, contests are spread across many Redis primaries by contest ID, and very large contests are sharded internally. Final results and payouts are computed from the durable database, not from Redis, because Redis replication is asynchronous.

pitfalls.trap: Running KEYS * or a huge range query in production.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd use SCAN with a cursor and keep operations bounded; one slow command blocks the single command thread.'

pitfalls.trap: Using Redis as the system of record for money or orders.
pitfalls.say: 'Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes; the database is the source of truth.'

deep.diagram:
client -> CRC16(key) mod 16384 = slot 9842
slots 0-5460     -> primary A (+replica)
slots 5461-10922 -> primary B (+replica)   <- slot 9842
slots 10923-16383-> primary C (+replica)
takeaways: Redis executes commands on one thread in RAM: fast and atomic, but slow commands block everyone.
Pick the data structure for the job: sorted sets for rankings, hashes for objects, streams for logs.
Replication is asynchronous; persistence is optional. Don't make Redis your only copy of critical data.
Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 slots; use hash tags to co-locate related keys.

mechanism.title: How to choose a database from access patterns, step by step
steps: Write down the entities and the five to ten queries the product must serve, with rough rates: 'get order by id, 2,000/s', 'list a user's orders newest first, 500/s', 'monthly revenue by city, once a day'.

Mark which operations must change several rows atomically (move money, reserve a seat and create a booking). These want ACID transactions across rows or tables, which relational databases give you by default.
Mark which queries need joins or ad hoc filters you cannot predict yet. SQL handles unknown future queries well because the schema is normalised and the planner can combine tables.

Estimate data size and write rate. A single well-tuned Postgres or MySQL primary on modern hardware comfortably serves a few terabytes and thousands of writes per second; most products never outgrow that.

Only if one machine clearly cannot hold the data or absorb the writes, or the access pattern is a pure key lookup at huge scale, consider a NoSQL family: key-value for lookups by id, document for self-contained nested records, wide-column for very high write rates partitioned by key, graph for many-hop relationship queries.
Validate the choice against the hardest query, not the easiest one, and say what you give up (joins, multi-row transactions, flexible queries) if you pick NoSQL.

useWhen: Money, inventory, bookings and anything with multi-row invariants: use a relational database with transactions.
Huge write-heavy streams read by a known key (sensor readings, chat messages by conversation, activity feeds): a wide-column or key-value store partitioned by that key fits.
avoidWhen: Do not pick NoSQL 'because it scales' when the data is a few hundred gigabytes and relational; you lose joins and transactions for capacity you do not need.
Do not force a relational schema onto highly variable records that are always read whole, such as product attribute bags that differ by category; a document model or a JSONB column is simpler.

rows: Horizontal write scaling needs sharding work
Single-key get/put at very high rates
Queries by anything except the key
Nested records read and written whole

numbers.title: Does one SQL primary fit?
assumptions: 10 million users, 20 orders each per year, 2 KB per order row with indexes
Peak 3,000 order writes per second during a sale
steps: Storage per year = 200,000,000 × 2 KB = 400,000,000 KB, which is about 400 GB.
Five years of orders is about 2 TB: large, but within what one primary with replicas can hold on modern SSDs.
3,000 writes per second is within reach of one tuned primary with batching and good indexes; reads go to replicas and caches.
numbers.result: A single relational primary plus read replicas fits this workload for years. Shard or move a specific table to NoSQL only when measured growth says one machine will not cope.

india.title: A kirana-ordering app's catalogue and orders
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Imagine a quick-commerce app in Bengaluru. Orders, payments and stock reservations live in Postgres, because confirming an order must atomically decrement stock in one dark store and create the order; a partial write would sell items that are not on the shelf. Product details, though, vary wildly by category: atta has weight and brand, a phone charger has wattage and connector type. Those attribute bags are stored as a JSON document per product, either in a document store or in a JSONB column, and served through a cache. The live delivery-partner location stream, many small writes per second keyed by rider id, goes to a key-value or wide-column store with a short retention. Three stores, each chosen by its access pattern, not by fashion.

pitfalls.trap: 'I'll use MongoDB because it scales better.'
pitfalls.say: 'Orders need multi-row transactions and joins, and two terabytes fits one Postgres primary with replicas, so I'd start relational and move only the location stream to a key-value store.'

pitfalls.trap: Naming a database before listing the queries.
pitfalls.say: 'Let me list the access patterns and rates first, then pick a store per pattern.'

takeaways: Choose by access pattern, invariants and size, not by brand.
One relational primary with replicas covers far more scale than most designs need.
NoSQL trades joins and multi-row transactions for partitioned scale; say that trade out loud.
Mixed workloads often deserve two or three stores, each with a clear job.

mechanism.title: Query-first modelling in a partitioned NoSQL store
steps: List every query with its filter and sort, for example 'messages in conversation C, newest first, 50 at a time'.
Choose the partition key from the equality filter of the main query (conversation_id). All rows with the same partition key live together on one node, so the query reads one partition.
Choose the sort (clustering) key from the ordering you need (message timestamp or a time-ordered id). Inside the partition rows are stored sorted, so 'newest 50' is a contiguous range read.

For each extra query with a different filter, create another table or a secondary index keyed for that query, and write to both. Duplicating data is normal; joins at read time are not available or are expensive.

Check partition size and heat: a single partition should stay well below the store's comfortable limit (tens to low hundreds of megabytes in Cassandra guidance) and should not take a large share of all traffic.
If one key is too big or too hot, add a bucket to the key, such as (conversation_id, month) or (item_id, shard 0–9), and read the buckets you need.

useWhen: The queries are known and stable, and each can be answered by one partition.
Write volume or data size is beyond a single machine and you can live without joins.
avoidWhen: Queries are ad hoc or change weekly (analytics, admin search): put that data in SQL, a warehouse or a search index instead.
You need invariants across many partitions, such as a uniqueness check across all users, without a separate coordination step.

rows: Even spread, one-partition reads per user
