sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: What an API gateway does to each request
steps: Terminates TLS for the public domain and normalises the request (headers, request id).
Authenticates the caller: validates the JWT or session, or the API key, and attaches identity claims for downstream services.
Applies cross-cutting policy: rate limits per user or key, request size limits, IP allow or deny lists, and CORS.
Routes by path, host or version to the right internal service, often through service discovery, with timeouts and retries.
Optionally aggregates: a backend-for-frontend (BFF) endpoint calls several services in parallel and returns one response shaped for the mobile app.
Records metrics, logs and the trace id, so every downstream call can be correlated.

useWhen: One public entry point for many internal services, with consistent authentication, rate limiting and observability.
A BFF per client type when mobile and web need differently shaped responses.
avoidWhen: Do not put business logic (pricing rules, order validation) in the gateway; it becomes a shared monolith every team must change, and every release of it risks every API.
Do not chain many sequential downstream calls in an aggregation endpoint; parallelise or move the composition into a service.

numbers.title: Latency of an aggregation endpoint
assumptions: Home screen needs profile (30 ms), offers (50 ms) and orders (80 ms)
steps: Sequential calls: 30 + 50 + 80 = 160 ms, plus 3 ms overhead, so 163 ms.
Parallel calls: the slowest dominates, so 80 ms plus 3 ms = 83 ms.
If offers is optional, a 60 ms timeout with a fallback (empty carousel) caps its effect on the page.
Then the page waits for the slower of profile (30 ms) and orders (80 ms), still 83 ms; to go faster, orders itself must get quicker or be loaded after first paint.
numbers.result: Parallel fan-out in a BFF roughly halves this screen's latency from 163 ms to 83 ms; timeouts keep optional parts from dragging it out.

india.title: Mobile home screen of a super-app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian super-app's home screen shows wallet balance, recharge shortcuts, offers, recent transactions and movie tickets. Making the phone call five services over a patchy 4G connection would cost five round trips at maybe 100 ms each. Instead, a mobile BFF behind the gateway accepts one request, calls the services in parallel inside the data centre where each hop is a few milliseconds, applies timeouts and fallbacks (offers can be skipped), and returns one compact JSON payload. The gateway in front handles authentication and rate limits once for all of them.

pitfalls.trap: Putting discount calculation in the gateway.
pitfalls.say: 'The gateway handles authentication, rate limits and routing; pricing lives in the pricing service so its team owns it.'

pitfalls.trap: Making the gateway a single point of failure.
pitfalls.say: 'The gateway runs as several stateless instances behind a load balancer across zones, and its config is versioned and rolled out like code.'

pitfalls.trap: Treating the gateway as authorisation for everything.
pitfalls.say: 'The gateway checks the token and scopes; each service still checks that this user may access this resource.'

takeaways: The gateway centralises TLS, auth, rate limiting, routing and tracing.
Keep business logic in services, not the gateway.
BFF endpoints aggregate in parallel with timeouts and fallbacks.
Services still enforce fine-grained authorisation.

title: Service Discovery
objectives: Explain why services need discovery
Compare client-side and server-side discovery
Keep registries accurate with heartbeats

cards.title: The problem
cards.body: Instances come and go with autoscaling and deploys, so their addresses change. Callers need a live list of healthy instances for each service.

cards.title: Registries
cards.body: Instances register with a registry (Consul, etcd, Eureka) on start and send heartbeats; dead ones expire. In Kubernetes, a Service and its DNS name do this for you.

cards.title: Client-side vs server-side
cards.body: Client-side discovery: the caller asks the registry and picks an instance itself. Server-side: the caller hits a load balancer or DNS name, which picks for it. Server-side keeps clients simple.

cards.title: A call with discovery
cards.body: 5 steps from “Instance starts and registers” to “Caller calls one; dead instances expire from the list”, via “It sends heartbeats”.
steps: Instance starts and registers
It sends heartbeats
Caller looks up “payments”
Registry returns healthy instances
Caller calls one; dead instances expire from the list

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Hard-coding IPs in config, or caching lookups with no refresh. Deploys then send traffic to instances that no longer exist.

mechanism.title: How a call finds a healthy instance
steps: Instances register themselves (or are registered by the platform) in a registry such as Consul, Eureka or the Kubernetes API, with address, port and health.
Health checks remove instances that fail, and a time-to-live or heartbeat removes ones that vanish without deregistering.
Client-side discovery: the caller's library asks the registry for instances of 'payments', caches the list and picks one itself (round robin, least requests).
Server-side discovery: the caller sends to a stable address (a load balancer or proxy), which looks up healthy instances and forwards the request.

In Kubernetes, a Service gets a stable DNS name such as payments.prod.svc.cluster.local and a virtual IP; kube-proxy or the CNI forwards traffic to the ready pods selected by labels, using the endpoints the control plane maintains.
A service mesh (Envoy sidecars with Istio or Linkerd) moves discovery, retries and mTLS into a proxy next to each pod.

useWhen: Any environment where instances come and go: autoscaling groups, containers, rolling deploys.
Kubernetes Services for most in-cluster traffic; a registry or mesh for multi-cluster or mixed environments.
avoidWhen: Do not hard-code IP addresses or instance lists in configuration files.
Do not rely on DNS alone when record TTLs and client caching delay removal of dead instances; combine it with health checks and retries.

numbers.title: How quickly a dead instance stops getting traffic
assumptions: Health check every 5 s, 3 failures to mark unhealthy
Clients refresh their instance list every 10 s
steps: Detection time = 5 × 3 = 15 seconds.
Clients may keep using a cached list for up to 10 more seconds, so worst case about 25 seconds.
At 400 requests per second to that service with 10 instances, the dead one receives about 40 per second, so about 40 × 25 = 1,000 failed requests without retries.
Retries to another instance on connection failure turn most of those into slightly slower successes.
numbers.result: Detection plus cache refresh sets how long a dead instance gets traffic; retries on another instance hide most of the damage.

india.title: Payments pods during a rolling deploy
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During a rolling deploy of a payments service running on Kubernetes in an Indian cloud region, old pods are terminated and new ones start. Callers never see pod IPs: they call payments.prod.svc.cluster.local. A new pod receives traffic only after its readiness probe passes, and a terminating pod is removed from the endpoints first and given a short grace period to finish in-flight requests. Without readiness probes, new pods still loading configuration would receive traffic and fail requests in the middle of the busiest hour.

pitfalls.trap: Hard-coding service addresses.
pitfalls.say: 'Services call a stable name; the registry or Kubernetes Service maps it to healthy instances.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring the time to detect failures.
pitfalls.say: 'With 5-second checks and 3 failures, detection takes 15 seconds, so callers also retry on another instance.'

takeaways: Discovery maps a stable name to the current healthy instances.
Client-side saves a hop; server-side keeps clients simple.
Kubernetes Services plus readiness probes cover most in-cluster cases.
Detection delay plus cache refresh decides how long dead instances get traffic.

pod -> registers/ready -> [ registry / k8s endpoints ]
caller -> payments.svc (DNS/VIP) -> kube-proxy -> ready pod

title: Timeouts/Retries/Circuit Breakers
objectives: Set timeouts that fit the caller’s deadline
Retry safely without multiplying load
Use circuit breakers and bulkheads to contain failures

cards.title: Timeouts
cards.body: Every outbound call needs a timeout shorter than the caller’s own deadline. Without one, threads wait forever on a hung dependency and the caller runs out of threads too.

cards.title: Retries
cards.body: Retry only idempotent operations, a few times, with exponential backoff and jitter. Retries at every layer multiply: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers is up to 27 calls.

cards.title: Circuit breakers
cards.body: Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: after too many failures, calls fail fast without trying. Half-open: after a cooldown, a few trial calls decide whether to close again.

cards.title: A breaker through an outage
cards.body: 5 steps from “Closed: calls flow” to “Trials succeed: closed again”, via “Failures pass the threshold”.
steps: Closed: calls flow
Failures pass the threshold
Open: fail fast
Cooldown, then half-open trial calls
Trials succeed: closed again

cards.title: Bulkheads
cards.body: Give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so a slow recommendations service cannot use up the pool checkout needs.

choices.label: Closed: all calls flow at once

flashcards.back: Half-open: a few trial calls. Trials decide whether to close.

flashcards.back: Its threads pile up waiting until it cannot serve anyone. Hung calls spread the outage upward.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How the resilience patterns work together
steps: Timeout: every outbound call gets a deadline based on the dependency's normal p99 (for example 300 ms). Without one, a hung dependency holds threads forever.
Retry: retry only idempotent or idempotency-keyed operations, only on transient errors, with exponential backoff and jitter, and with a retry budget (for example at most 10% extra traffic).
Circuit breaker, closed state: calls flow, and the breaker tracks the error rate over a window.
Open state: when errors pass a threshold (say 50% over 20 or more calls), the breaker fails calls immediately or serves a fallback for a cool-down period, giving the dependency room to recover.
Half-open state: after the cool-down, a few trial calls are allowed; success closes the breaker, failure opens it again.
Bulkhead: separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency, so a slow recommendations service cannot exhaust the threads that checkout needs.

useWhen: Every network call between services, to databases and to third-party APIs.
Breakers and fallbacks around non-critical dependencies (recommendations, reviews) so the core flow survives their failure.
avoidWhen: Do not retry at every layer of a deep call chain; retries multiply.
Do not retry non-idempotent writes such as payments without an idempotency key.

rows: Too short: false failures; too long: thread exhaustion
Retry storms that amplify an outage
Opening too eagerly on small samples
Pools sized too small waste capacity
Stale or default data shown silently

numbers.title: How retries multiply in a call chain
assumptions: Three layers: gateway calls A, A calls B, B calls the database
Each layer makes 1 attempt plus up to 2 retries (3 attempts)
steps: If the database is down, B tries it 3 times for each call from A.
A tries B 3 times, so the database sees 3 × 3 = 9 attempts per call from the gateway.
The gateway also tries 3 times, so 9 × 3 = 27 database attempts per user request.
Retrying only at one layer, or using a retry budget, keeps this at about 3.
numbers.result: Retries at every layer multiply: three layers of three attempts make 27 calls to a struggling database, so retry at one layer and use budgets.

india.title: Recommendations down during a sale
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During a festival sale, an e-commerce site's 'customers also bought' service slows to 5-second responses under load. Without timeouts, product page threads wait on it and the whole page, including Add to Cart, stops responding. With a 200 ms timeout, a circuit breaker that opens once more than half of calls fail, and a bulkhead limiting recommendations to its own small pool, the product page renders without recommendations and sales continue. When the breaker's half-open trial calls succeed a minute later, the carousel quietly returns.

pitfalls.trap: 'I'll add retries to make it reliable.'
pitfalls.say: 'Retries can turn an outage into a storm; I'd retry only idempotent calls at one layer with backoff, jitter and a budget, behind a circuit breaker.'

pitfalls.trap: No timeout on outbound calls.
pitfalls.say: 'Every call has a timeout based on the dependency's p99, and the caller's deadline is propagated downstream.'

takeaways: Every remote call needs a timeout.
Retry idempotent calls with backoff, jitter and a budget, at one layer.
Circuit breakers fail fast and let dependencies recover.
Bulkheads stop one slow dependency from starving the rest.

CLOSED --errors > 50%--> OPEN (fail fast / fallback) --cool-down--> HALF-OPEN

   +-------------------- trial calls succeed -----------------------+

objectives: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Request gets trace ID” to “Dashboards & alerts”, via “Each service logs it”.
steps: Request gets trace ID
Each service logs it
Spans recorded

cards.title: Watch out for

choices.label: Grepping each service’s logs by timestamp

questions.explanation: Spans show time spent per hop.

questions.explanation: Service-level health in three numbers.

choices.label: Saturation, such as the I/O queue depth
Requests per second to the API

questions.explanation: The trace id ties it together.

99% of requests are faster than this.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Following one request through logs, metrics and traces
steps: At the edge, the gateway assigns a trace id (W3C traceparent header) and passes it to every downstream call.
Each service creates spans (start time, duration, status) for its work and outbound calls, tagged with the trace id; a tracing backend (Jaeger, Tempo, Zipkin) assembles them into a waterfall.

Metrics: each service exports counters and histograms, such as RED for request-driven services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE for resources (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors). Dashboards and alerts read these.
Logs: structured JSON lines with timestamp, level, service, trace id and key fields, never secrets or full card numbers.
Debugging flow: an alert fires on the p99 duration metric, a trace shows which span is slow, and the logs for that trace id explain why.
Sampling keeps cost in check: keep all error traces and a small percentage of successful ones.
Alerts fire on symptoms users feel, such as error rate and p99 latency against the SLO, rather than on every CPU spike, so on-call engineers are woken only for real problems.

useWhen: Metrics for alerting and trends: cheap, aggregated, kept long.
Traces for finding where time goes in a multi-service request; logs for the detailed why.
avoidWhen: Do not log every request body at high volume; cost explodes and sensitive data leaks.
Do not use high-cardinality labels such as user_id on metrics; each unique value creates a new time series.

numbers.title: Log volume and the case for sampling
assumptions: Each request logs 4 lines of 500 bytes
steps: Lines per second = 5,000 × 4 = 20,000.
Bytes per second = 20,000 × 500 = 10,000,000, about 10 MB per second.
Per day = 10 MB × 86,400 ≈ 864 GB.
Keeping 14 days needs about 12 TB, before replication.
Logging one line per request at info level and sampling debug logs at 1% cuts this by about 4×.
numbers.result: Verbose logging at 5,000 requests per second produces close to a terabyte a day; decide levels and sampling up front.

india.title: Finding a slow UPI checkout
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian e-commerce team gets an alert: checkout p99 latency has jumped from 800 ms to 4 s. The RED dashboard shows the error rate is normal, so requests are slow rather than failing. A sampled trace shows the payment-initiation span taking 3.2 s, and inside it a call to a bank's UPI collect endpoint. The logs for that trace id show repeated retries after timeouts from one bank's API. The team tightens the timeout, routes users of that bank to the intent flow, and updates the status page. Without a shared trace id, the same investigation could have taken hours of grepping across services.

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll add logging.'
pitfalls.say: 'I'd emit RED metrics per endpoint for alerts, propagate a trace id across services, and write structured logs keyed by that id.'

pitfalls.trap: Sampling away the traces you need.
pitfalls.say: 'I keep every error trace and every trace slower than the SLO threshold, and sample only a small share of fast successful ones.'

pitfalls.trap: Putting user_id on metrics labels.
pitfalls.say: 'High-cardinality ids go in logs and traces; metrics labels stay low-cardinality like endpoint and status code.'

takeaways: Metrics alert, traces locate, logs explain.
Propagate one trace id end to end.
Use RED for services and USE for resources.
Control cost with sampling and low-cardinality labels; never log secrets.

title: Availability & SLAs
objectives: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year down, 99.99% ≈ 53 min/year. Components in series multiply availability (lower); redundant components in parallel raise it. SLO = internal target; SLA = contractual promise.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Single node” to “Health checks + failover”, via “Find SPOFs”.
steps: Single node
Find SPOFs
Add replicas
Spread across zones
Health checks + failover

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Claiming five nines without redundancy across zones. Availability comes from removing single points of failure.

questions.prompt: Two services in series, each 99.9% available. End-to-end availability?
questions.explanation: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, assuming independent failures.

questions.prompt: Allowed downtime per year at 99.9% availability, in hours?
Two independent replicas, each 99% available, with instant failover. Availability?
questions.explanation: Both must fail: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999.

questions.prompt: SLO versus SLA?

choices.label: SLA is measured per request, SLO per year
SLO is the internal target; SLA is the promise to customers, with penalties
SLA is the internal target; SLO is the customer promise

questions.explanation: Set the SLO tighter than the SLA.

questions.prompt: Order the path to higher availability.
questions.explanation: Remove single points of failure step by step.

questions.prompt: Three components each at 99.9% availability are in series. What is the system availability?
questions.explanation: 0.999 cubed is about 0.997: series components multiply.

flashcards.back: ≈ 52.6 minutes.
Series multiplies (lower); parallel redundancy raises it.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Computing availability for a whole system
steps: Convert each target into allowed downtime: 99.9% of a 30-day month is 0.1% of 43,200 minutes, about 43 minutes.
Components in series (all must work): multiply availabilities. Three dependencies at 99.9% give about 99.7%.
Components in parallel (any one is enough): the system fails only if all fail. Two independent copies at 99% fail together 1% × 1% of the time, giving 99.99%.
Find single points of failure: any series component without redundancy, such as one database primary, one DNS provider or one region.

Set an SLO (internal target, for example 99.95% of checkout requests succeed within 1 s over 30 days) and an error budget (the remaining 0.05%). The SLA is the contractual promise, set looser than the SLO, with credits if broken.
Spend the error budget on releases and experiments; if it runs out, slow down changes and fix reliability.

useWhen: Use the series and parallel maths to decide where redundancy buys the most.
Use SLOs and error budgets to balance shipping speed against reliability.
avoidWhen: Do not promise more nines than your dependencies allow; a system cannot beat its series chain without redundancy.
Do not assume redundant copies fail independently if they share a power feed, zone, deploy or bug.

numbers.title: Series and parallel worked example
assumptions: Load balancer 99.99%, app tier 99.9%, database 99.9%, all in series
Then make the database a primary plus a standby with automatic failover, treated as two 99.9% copies
steps: Two database copies in parallel fail together 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001 of the time, so about 99.9999%.
The weakest series link (the app tier at 99.9%) now limits the system; adding redundancy there is the next step.
numbers.result: Series chains multiply down; parallel redundancy multiplies failure probabilities, so fix the weakest series link first.

india.title: UPI apps and bank downtime
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A UPI payment involves the payer's app, the payer's bank, NPCI's switch and the payee's bank, all in series. Even if each were 99.9% available, four in series would give about 99.6%, which is roughly 2.9 hours of failure a month for some route. That is why payment apps show 'bank server down, try another account': they cannot add redundancy to someone else's bank, but they can let the user switch to a parallel path, another linked account. NPCI also publishes bank-wise technical decline rates, which is publicly reported data that shows this chain in practice.

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll have five nines.'
pitfalls.say: 'With a single database in series at 99.9%, the system cannot exceed about 99.9%; I'd add failover and measure an SLO of 99.95% first.'

pitfalls.trap: Assuming two replicas in the same zone are independent.
pitfalls.say: 'Copies that share a zone, power feed or deploy fail together, so I place them in different zones and stagger deploys.'

pitfalls.trap: Mixing up SLO and SLA.
pitfalls.say: 'The SLO is our internal target with an error budget; the SLA is the looser contractual promise with penalties.'

takeaways: Series availabilities multiply down.
Parallel redundancy multiplies failure probabilities together.
Translate nines into minutes of downtime.
SLO plus error budget guides how fast to ship; SLA is the contract.

title: Disaster Recovery & Multi-Region
objectives: Define RPO and RTO and derive them from business needs
Choose a disaster-recovery strategy
Explain the data cost of cross-region replication

cards.title: RPO and RTO
cards.body: RPO: how much data you can lose, measured in time (the last 5 minutes of writes). RTO: how long until service is back. Both are business decisions that set the design and the cost.

cards.title: Strategies
cards.body: Backup and restore: cheapest, hours of RTO. Pilot light: data replicated, minimal servers ready to scale. Warm standby: a smaller full copy running. Active-active: every region serves traffic; lowest RTO, hardest consistency.

steps: Mumbai region fails health checks
DNS or a global load balancer shifts traffic

Capacity scales up
Fail back after the incident

cards.title: Data across regions
cards.body: Async replication between regions keeps writes fast but means RPO above zero: the last seconds of writes can be lost. Synchronous cross-region writes give RPO zero at tens of ms per write.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Never testing failover. Backups that were never restored and runbooks that were never run tend to fail on the day. Rehearse with game days.

flashcards.back: An RPO of 5 minutes. RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.

flashcards.front: Cheapest DR strategy when hours of RTO are acceptable?
flashcards.back: Backup and restore. Nothing runs until you need it.

flashcards.back: The last seconds of writes may be lost (RPO above zero). Async trades a small data-loss window for fast writes.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Planning disaster recovery from RPO and RTO
steps: Define RPO (recovery point objective): how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. Define RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can be down.
Backup and restore: periodic backups to another region. Cheapest; RPO equals the backup interval, RTO is hours to rebuild and restore.
Pilot light: data continuously replicated to a second region with minimal infrastructure running; scale it up on failover. RPO of seconds to minutes, RTO of tens of minutes.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but running copy of the full stack in the second region. RTO of minutes.
Active-active: both regions serve traffic; failover is shifting traffic. RTO near zero, but writes need conflict handling or per-user home regions.

Failover itself: detect, decide (often a human for regional failover), promote the database, shift DNS or global load balancing, then verify. Rehearse it with game days, because untested failover usually fails.

useWhen: Tier systems by business impact: payments and orders get warm standby or active-active; internal reporting gets backup and restore.
Regulated data must also satisfy data-residency rules, such as keeping payment data in India under RBI rules (publicly reported), which shapes where the DR region can be.
avoidWhen: Do not pay for active-active everywhere; it doubles cost and adds write-conflict complexity for systems that tolerate an hour of downtime.
Do not count on a DR plan that has never been rehearsed.

numbers.title: What an RPO means in lost orders
assumptions: Option A: 15-minute snapshots; option B: asynchronous replication with about 5 seconds of lag
steps: Option A worst case loses up to 15 minutes: 2,000 × 15 = 30,000 orders.
Option B loses about 5 seconds: 2,000 × 5 ÷ 60 ≈ 167 orders.
Synchronous cross-region replication would lose none but adds the inter-region round trip to every commit.
Lost orders still have payment records at the gateway, so reconciliation is needed either way.
numbers.result: RPO translates directly into lost business events; continuous replication shrinks 30,000 lost orders to a couple of hundred.

india.title: Regional outage for a brokerage app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A stock-broking app in India cannot be down during market hours, 9:15 to 15:30 IST, when a few minutes of outage can trigger customer losses and regulatory scrutiny. It might run warm standby across two Indian cloud regions, such as Mumbai and Hyderabad, replicating order and ledger data continuously, and rehearse failover monthly on a weekend. Because the exchanges are the source of truth for executed trades, reconciliation after failover compares the app's records with exchange trade files to fill any gap left by replication lag. Back-office reporting, by contrast, uses nightly backups.

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll be multi-region.'
pitfalls.say: 'Our RPO is under a minute and RTO under 15 minutes for orders, so I'd use warm standby with async replication; reporting uses backups.'

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting to test failover.
pitfalls.say: 'We'd rehearse regional failover quarterly with game days and measure the actual RTO.'

takeaways: RPO is tolerable data loss; RTO is tolerable downtime.
Strategies trade cost for lower RPO and RTO.
Tier systems by impact instead of one plan for all.
Rehearse failover; untested DR is a guess.

region A (primary) --async replication (lag ~5 s)--> region B (warm standby)
 failure: detect -> decide -> promote DB in B -> shift DNS/GSLB -> verify -> reconcile

objectives: Prove who the user is: server sessions, signed tokens, or delegated OAuth/OIDC.

cards.body: Sessions store state server-side (easy revoke). JWTs are signed, stateless, short-lived with refresh tokens. OAuth 2.0 delegates access; OIDC adds identity.

Verify
Issue access + refresh

cards.body: Long-lived JWTs with no revocation path.

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.body: Authentication answers who you are (password, OTP, passkey, Sign in with Google). Authorization answers what you may do: can this user refund this order? Authenticate once per session; authorize on every request, close to the data.

questions.explanation: They proved who they are; they lacked permission for this action.

choices.label: They cannot be verified without the auth server
They are hard to revoke before they expire
They are too small to carry claims

questions.explanation: Nothing server-side remembers them.

questions.prompt: Why might a bank prefer server-side sessions over JWTs?

choices.label: A session can be revoked instantly by deleting it on the server
Every service verifies sessions without a lookup

questions.explanation: Server state makes revocation easy.

questions.prompt: Order a token-based login.

items.label: Call APIs with the access token

questions.explanation: Short access tokens, longer refresh tokens.

questions.prompt: Where should “can this user refund this order?” be checked?

choices.label: In the service that owns orders, on every request

questions.explanation: UI checks are convenience; the service enforces.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user changes the order id in a URL and sees someone else's order. Which check failed?
questions.explanation: The user was correctly authenticated, but the service did not check that the order belongs to them.

flashcards.back: Long-lived token to get new short-lived access tokens.
Who you are vs what you can do.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: From login to an authorised request
steps: Authentication (who are you?): the user proves identity with a password plus OTP, a passkey, or a login through an identity provider.

The server then issues a credential for later requests: either a session id stored server-side (in Redis or a database) and sent as an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, or a signed access token such as a JWT.
On each request the server authenticates the credential: look up the session id, or verify the token's signature, expiry, issuer and audience.
Authorisation (what may you do?): check the identity against rules: roles (RBAC, such as 'support agent'), attributes (ABAC, such as 'same branch'), or ownership ('order 123 belongs to user 42').
Authorisation runs on every request and every resource, inside the service that owns the data, not only once at login or at the gateway.
Logout or revocation: delete the server-side session immediately; for stateless tokens, keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 minutes) and revoke the refresh token, or check a deny-list.

useWhen: Server-side sessions for web apps where instant logout and revocation matter, such as banking.
Short-lived tokens for APIs and mobile apps calling many services, where each service verifies locally without a session lookup.
avoidWhen: Do not treat a valid login as permission to access any record; that is how insecure direct object reference (IDOR) bugs happen.
Do not issue long-lived JWTs (days) with no revocation path for sensitive apps.

rows: Revocation lists or short certificate lifetimes

numbers.title: Revocation window of a stolen token
assumptions: Attacker steals a token at a random moment
steps: Remaining lifetime is uniformly between 0 and 15 minutes, so on average 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 minutes of misuse.
With a 60-minute lifetime the average window is 60 ÷ 2 = 30 minutes.
With server-side sessions, deleting the session ends misuse on the next request.
Adding a deny-list check for high-risk actions (transfers) closes the window for those actions at the cost of one lookup.
numbers.result: Token lifetime is the revocation window; keep it short and add server-side checks for sensitive actions.

india.title: Netbanking and support consoles
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian bank's netbanking site typically uses server-side sessions with short idle timeouts, so 'log out' or 'session expired' takes effect immediately, and high-value actions such as adding a beneficiary need a fresh OTP (step-up authentication). Inside the bank, a support agent who has logged in successfully (authenticated) may view a customer's profile only for customers assigned to their branch and only certain fields (authorised by role and attributes), and every access is logged for audit. Authentication answers 'is this Priya from the Pune branch?'; authorisation answers 'may Priya see this account?'.

pitfalls.trap: 'The gateway checks the JWT, so services are secure.'
pitfalls.say: 'The gateway authenticates; each service still authorises, for example checking that order 123 belongs to this user.'

pitfalls.trap: 'JWTs can't be revoked, so we'll make them last a week.'
pitfalls.say: 'Access tokens last 15 minutes, refresh tokens are stored and revocable, and sensitive actions check a deny-list.'

takeaways: Authentication proves identity; authorisation decides access.
Authorise every request against the specific resource.
Sessions revoke instantly; short tokens bound the damage window.
Step-up authentication protects high-risk actions.
deep.diagram:
login (password + OTP) -> issue session cookie / JWT
request -> authenticate credential -> authorise (role? owner? scope?) -> allow / 403

cards.body: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on your behalf with limited scopes (“read my Google Drive files”). OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top so the app also learns who you are: “Sign in with Google”.

cards.title: Code flow with PKCE
cards.body: The app redirects to the identity provider, gets a short-lived code back, and exchanges it, plus a PKCE verifier, for tokens over a back channel. PKCE stops a stolen code being redeemed by another app.

Google redirects back with a code

flashcards.back: The OIDC ID token.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Authorization Code flow with PKCE, step by step
steps: The app generates a random code_verifier and sends its SHA-256 hash (code_challenge) when redirecting the user to the authorisation server with client_id, redirect_uri, requested scopes and a random state value.
The user signs in at the authorisation server (for example Google) and approves the requested scopes, such as 'openid email calendar.readonly'.
The authorisation server redirects back to redirect_uri with a short-lived authorisation code and the same state, which the app checks to block cross-site request forgery.
The app exchanges the code plus the original code_verifier at the token endpoint. The server hashes the verifier and compares it with the challenge, so a stolen code alone is useless.

The response contains an access token (for calling APIs within the granted scopes), usually a refresh token, and with OpenID Connect an ID token: a signed JWT that says who the user is (sub, email, issuer, audience, expiry).
The app validates the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and nonce to log the user in, and sends the access token only to the resource API.

useWhen: OAuth 2.0 when your app needs delegated access to a user's data in another service with limited scopes.
OpenID Connect for 'Sign in with Google' and single sign-on; PKCE for every public client (mobile, single-page app) and recommended for all.
avoidWhen: Do not use the implicit flow or the password grant in new apps; both are discouraged by current OAuth security guidance.
Do not use an access token as proof of identity in your own app; use the ID token, which is meant for you.

numbers.title: Why PKCE makes a stolen code worthless
steps: To redeem the code, the attacker needs a verifier whose SHA-256 hash matches the challenge.
Guessing 256 random bits takes on the order of 2 to the power 255 tries on average.
Even at a trillion guesses per second, that is vastly longer than the code's lifetime of under a minute.
So intercepting the code through a malicious app on the phone gains nothing.
numbers.result: PKCE binds the code to a secret only the real app holds, which is why public clients must use it.

india.title: Sign in with Google and DigiLocker
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Many Indian apps offer 'Sign in with Google', which is OpenID Connect: the app receives an ID token proving the user's Google identity and email, and never sees the password. DigiLocker publicly documents an OAuth 2.0 based API through which partner apps, after the user's consent, can fetch issued documents such as a driving licence for KYC. That is delegated authorisation: the user grants a specific scope to a specific app, can revoke it, and the app never learns the user's DigiLocker credentials. The details of each provider's scopes are in their public documentation.

pitfalls.trap: 'OAuth is for login.'
pitfalls.say: 'OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorisation; OpenID Connect adds the ID token for login.'

pitfalls.trap: Skipping PKCE in a mobile app.
pitfalls.say: 'Mobile apps are public clients, so I'd use the authorisation code flow with PKCE and check state and nonce.'

takeaways: OAuth delegates scoped access; OIDC adds identity via the ID token.
Use authorisation code with PKCE for all public clients.
Request the narrowest scopes needed.
Validate ID tokens: signature, issuer, audience, expiry, nonce.
deep.diagram:
app --(challenge, scopes, state)--> auth server --login + consent--> redirect ?code&state
app --(code + verifier)--> token endpoint --> access token, refresh token, ID token

title: JWT
objectives: Explain what a JWT contains and who can read it
Weigh stateless tokens against revocation
Pick sensible token lifetimes

cards.title: Signed, not secret
cards.body: A JWT is header.payload.signature, base64-encoded. Anyone holding it can read the claims; the signature only proves they were not changed. Never put secrets in the payload.

cards.title: Why services like it
cards.body: Any service with the public key can verify a token without calling the auth server, so verification scales horizontally and survives an auth outage.

cards.title: Verifying a request
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client sends Authorization: Bearer token” to “Passes user claims to service”, via “Gateway checks signature with public key”.
steps: Client sends Authorization: Bearer token
Gateway checks signature with public key
Checks exp, aud, iss
Passes user claims to service

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Week-long access tokens. A stateless token cannot be easily revoked, so keep access tokens short (minutes) and use refresh tokens, which can be revoked server-side.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to put the user’s PAN in the JWT payload “because it is signed”. What is wrong?

choices.label: Anyone holding the token can decode it; signing only stops changes
Only the gateway can read the payload
The token becomes too large to sign

questions.explanation: Signed, not secret.

questions.prompt: A user logs out but their access token is valid for 7 more days. Which design limits this best?

choices.label: Short-lived access tokens with revocable refresh tokens

questions.explanation: Keep the window of a stolen token small.

questions.prompt: Why can 20 services verify JWTs without overloading the auth server?

choices.label: The auth server pushes sessions to all of them
Each verifies the signature with the public key, without a call
Tokens are verified only at login

questions.explanation: Verification is local.

questions.prompt: Order JWT verification at the gateway.

items.label: Gateway checks the signature with the public key
Gateway checks exp, aud and iss
Gateway passes user claims to the service

questions.explanation: Signature first, then claims.

questions.prompt: Besides the signature, what should verification check?
questions.explanation: A valid signature on an expired or foreign token is still a reject.

questions.prompt: Why should a PAN number not be placed in a JWT payload?

choices.label: The payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it
It makes the token expire sooner

questions.explanation: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality; the payload is readable by anyone.

flashcards.front: Can anyone read a JWT payload?
flashcards.back: Yes. It is signed, not encrypted.

flashcards.front: Why are JWTs easy to scale?
flashcards.back: Services verify them locally with a public key, no auth-server call.

flashcards.front: How do you limit damage from a stolen JWT?
flashcards.back: Short expiry plus revocable refresh tokens.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: What happens when a service verifies a JWT
steps: A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots: header (algorithm, key id), payload (claims) and signature. Base64url is encoding, not encryption, so anyone can read the payload.
The service splits the token and reads the header's alg and kid. It accepts only an allow-listed algorithm (for example RS256 or ES256), never 'none', and never lets the token choose.
It fetches the issuer's public key for that kid from a cached JWKS endpoint and verifies the signature over header and payload.
It checks claims: exp (not expired, with small clock-skew leeway), nbf, iss (expected issuer), aud (this service is the intended audience).
Only then does it trust sub (user id) and scopes or roles in the payload, and authorise the request.
Because verification is local, no database call is needed, which is why JWTs scale well, and also why revocation before expiry needs extra machinery.

useWhen: Stateless authentication between many services, and short-lived access tokens from an identity provider.
Asymmetric signing (RS256 or ES256) when many services verify but only the issuer signs.
avoidWhen: Do not put secrets or personal data such as Aadhaar or PAN numbers in a JWT payload; it is readable by anyone holding it.
Do not use JWTs as long-lived web sessions when instant logout matters; server-side sessions are simpler.

rows: Every verifier can also forge tokens
Verifiers hold only the public key

numbers.title: Token size on every request
assumptions: JWT of about 900 bytes in the Authorization header
50,000 requests per second through the gateway
steps: Header bytes per second = 50,000 × 900 = 45,000,000, about 45 MB per second.
Per day = 45 MB × 86,400 ≈ 3.9 TB of header traffic.
Trimming claims to about 400 bytes saves roughly 2.2 TB a day.
Keep claims minimal: user id, scopes, expiry, issuer, audience.
numbers.result: JWTs travel on every request, so bloated claims cost real bandwidth; keep them small.

india.title: Tokens in a fintech mobile app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A mobile investment app issues 10-minute RS256 access tokens containing only the user id, scopes and expiry, plus a refresh token stored in the phone's secure keystore. Each microservice verifies tokens locally with keys fetched from the identity service's JWKS endpoint and cached for an hour. PAN and bank account details never appear in the token, because anyone who captures it, for example through a misconfigured log, could decode the payload. When a user reports a lost phone, support revokes the refresh token, and the access token dies within 10 minutes.

pitfalls.trap: Storing the access token in browser localStorage for a high-value web app.
pitfalls.say: 'Any XSS can read localStorage, so for the web I'd keep tokens in HttpOnly, Secure cookies or use a backend-for-frontend that holds them server-side.'

pitfalls.trap: 'JWTs are encrypted.'
pitfalls.say: 'A signed JWT is only encoded; anyone can read the claims, so no secrets go in it.'

pitfalls.trap: Trusting the alg in the token header.
pitfalls.say: 'The verifier pins the allowed algorithm and key, so a token claiming alg none or HS256 with the public key is rejected.'

takeaways: JWT payloads are readable; never put secrets in them.
Verify signature with a pinned algorithm, then exp, iss and aud.
Prefer asymmetric keys when many services verify.
Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens make revocation workable.

title: Security Essentials
objectives: Layer defences so one failure is not a breach
Prevent injection with parameterised queries
Handle secrets and permissions with least privilege

cards.title: Defence in depth
cards.body: Assume any one layer fails. Combine TLS in transit, authentication, authorization on every request, input validation, rate limits, encryption at rest and audit logs.

cards.title: Injection
cards.body: Never build SQL or shell commands from user input. Use parameterised queries, and validate input. One string-concatenated query can leak a whole table.

cards.title: Secrets
cards.body: Keep API keys and passwords out of code and images. Load them from a secrets manager at runtime, scope each to one service, and rotate them.

cards.title: A request through the layers
cards.body: 5 steps from “TLS at the edge” to “Validate input and run a parameterised query”, via “Rate limit and web firewall”.
steps: TLS at the edge
Rate limit and web firewall
Authenticate the token
Authorize this action
Validate input and run a parameterised query

cards.title: Least privilege
cards.body: Give each service and person only the access they need: a read-only database user for reporting, a bucket policy for one prefix. A breach then exposes less.

questions.prompt: Search builds SQL as "… WHERE name = '" + input + "'". Fix?

choices.label: Wrap the same concatenation in a stored procedure
Strip quotes from the input with a regex

questions.explanation: Parameters keep data from being parsed as SQL.

questions.prompt: Where should a payment-gateway API key live?

choices.label: In a secrets manager, loaded at runtime and rotated

questions.explanation: Code and images get copied; secrets must not travel with them.

questions.prompt: The reporting service only reads orders. Its database user should have:

choices.label: Read-only access to the tables it needs
Write access in case it needs it later

questions.explanation: Limit what a compromise can do.

questions.prompt: Order the layers a request passes through.
questions.explanation: Each layer catches what the previous missed.

choices.label: Not by itself: you still need authentication, authorization, validation and rate limits
Yes, once the CDN is enabled
Yes, as long as certificates are renewed

questions.explanation: TLS is one layer of several.

questions.prompt: A reporting service's database user can only SELECT from three tables. Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Granting only the access a component needs limits damage if it is compromised.

flashcards.front: Search builds SQL as "… WHERE name = '" + input + "'". Fix?

flashcards.front: Where should a payment-gateway API key live?
flashcards.back: In a secrets manager, loaded at runtime and rotated. Code and images get copied; secrets must not travel with them.

flashcards.front: The reporting service only reads orders. Its database user should have:
flashcards.back: Read-only access to the tables it needs. Limit what a compromise can do.

flashcards.front: HTTPS is enabled everywhere. Is the API secure?
flashcards.back: Not by itself: you still need authentication, authorization, validation and rate limits. TLS is one layer of several.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Layering defences around a typical web service
steps: Edge: TLS everywhere, a web application firewall and rate limits to absorb bots and common attacks.
Input handling: validate types and lengths, and use parameterised queries or an ORM so user input is never concatenated into SQL; encode output to prevent cross-site scripting.
Identity: strong authentication (OTP, passkeys), short-lived tokens, and authorisation checks on every resource.
Least privilege: each service has its own database user with only the tables and verbs it needs, and each cloud role only the actions it needs.
Secrets: kept in a secrets manager or vault, injected at runtime, rotated, never committed to Git or printed in logs.
Data: encrypt at rest and in transit, mask sensitive fields in logs, and keep audit logs; then monitor and alert on anomalies, and patch dependencies promptly.

useWhen: Defence in depth for any internet-facing system: assume one layer will fail.
Least privilege everywhere, so a compromised component can do limited harm.
avoidWhen: Do not rely on a single control such as the WAF or the gateway as the whole security story.
Do not roll your own cryptography or password hashing; use vetted libraries such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.

rows: Secrets manager, rotation, secret scanning in CI
Rate limits, OTP or passkeys, breached-password checks

numbers.title: Why slow password hashing matters
assumptions: Fast unsalted hash: about 10 billion guesses per second on GPUs (illustrative)
bcrypt at a cost giving about 10,000 guesses per second per GPU (illustrative)
steps: A list of the 1,000,000 most common passwords tried against an unsalted fast hash needs just one pass over the list for all users, about 0.0001 seconds of GPU time.
With per-user salts the attacker must hash each guess per user: 1,000,000 guesses × 1,000,000 users = 1,000,000,000,000 hashes.
At 10,000 bcrypt hashes per second, that is 100,000,000 seconds, about 3.2 years on one GPU.
Salting stops the shared pass, and a slow hash multiplies the cost per guess.
numbers.result: Salted, deliberately slow password hashing turns a fraction of a second into years of attacker work.

india.title: Lessons from leaked keys
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A common incident pattern, reported many times worldwide, is a developer committing cloud access keys to a public GitHub repository; automated scanners find such keys within minutes and use them to run crypto-miners or copy storage buckets. An Indian start-up preventing this would run secret scanning in CI, keep keys in a cloud secrets manager, give each service a narrowly scoped role instead of one admin key, and rotate keys regularly. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, organisations are also obliged to protect personal data with reasonable security safeguards, so these controls are legal hygiene as well as engineering hygiene.

pitfalls.trap: 'We have a firewall, so we're secure.'
pitfalls.say: 'I'd layer controls: WAF and rate limits at the edge, parameterised queries, per-resource authorisation, least-privilege roles and secrets in a vault.'

pitfalls.trap: Storing API keys in environment files in the repo.
pitfalls.say: 'Secrets live in a secrets manager, are injected at runtime, rotated, and CI blocks commits containing keys.'

takeaways: Assume any one control can fail; layer them.
Parameterised queries stop SQL injection.
Least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromise.
Secrets belong in a vault, never in code or logs.
deep.diagram:
internet -> [WAF + rate limit] -> [gateway: TLS, authn] -> [service: validate, authz] -> [DB user: least privilege]
 secrets from vault | logs masked | audit + alerts

objectives: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Object stores are durable (11 nines), cheap and scale infinitely. Clients upload directly with pre-signed URLs; metadata goes to a DB; processing runs async.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

Pre-signed URL
Direct upload to bucket

CDN serves

questions.prompt: Why use pre-signed URLs for uploads?

choices.label: Clients upload straight to the bucket, so large files skip your app servers

questions.explanation: The app only signs; the bucket receives the bytes.

questions.prompt: 1M uploads a day at 2 MB each. Storage added per year, in TB?
questions.workedAnswer: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB a day; 2 TB × 365 = 730 TB.
questions.explanation: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB a day; 2 TB × 365 = 730 TB.

questions.prompt: Why not store images as BLOBs in Postgres?

choices.label: Images would load faster from Postgres
It bloats the database, backups and replication; object storage is cheaper and built for it

questions.explanation: Keep the database for metadata.

questions.prompt: Order a media upload.

items.label: Client asks for an upload URL
Client uploads directly to the bucket

questions.explanation: Processing is asynchronous.

questions.prompt: Where do a photo’s owner, caption and object key go?

choices.label: In a database row that points at the object

questions.explanation: Objects hold bytes; the database holds what you query.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a presigned PUT URL for uploads?

choices.label: The client sends the file directly to object storage, bypassing app servers
It makes the file public forever
It stores the file inside the database
It removes the need for authorisation

questions.explanation: The app authorises and signs a short-lived URL; the bytes go straight to storage.

flashcards.back: Metadata in DB, bytes in object store.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: Uploading a file directly to object storage
steps: The client asks the app server for permission to upload 'profile.jpg, 2 MB, image/jpeg'.

The server authorises the user, checks the declared type and size, creates a metadata row (owner, key, status 'pending') and returns a presigned PUT URL valid for a few minutes, scoped to one object key and content type.
The client uploads the bytes straight to object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) using that URL, so the large payload never passes through the app servers.
Storage emits an event on completion, or the client confirms; a worker validates the file (real type, size, malware scan), creates thumbnails and marks the row 'ready'.
Downloads use short-lived presigned GET URLs or a CDN in front of a private bucket, never a public bucket by default.
Large files use multipart upload: parts of 5 MB or more are uploaded in parallel and retried individually, then combined.

useWhen: Images, videos, documents, backups and logs: large, immutable blobs.
Direct-to-storage uploads with presigned URLs whenever files are larger than a few hundred kilobytes.
avoidWhen: Do not store large blobs inside the database; backups, replication and the buffer cache all suffer.
Do not use object storage for small, frequently updated records; each write replaces the whole object and per-request costs add up.

rows: No partial updates, higher latency per request
Attached to one instance at a time

numbers.title: Bandwidth saved by presigned uploads
assumptions: 100,000 photo uploads per hour at 3 MB each
steps: Data per hour = 100,000 × 3 MB = 300,000 MB, which is 300 GB.
Per second = 300,000 MB ÷ 3,600 ≈ 83 MB per second, about 667 Mbit per second.
Proxying through app servers would add that much inbound and outbound traffic and tie up connections for each slow mobile upload.
With presigned URLs the app servers handle only small JSON requests.
numbers.result: Presigned direct uploads keep about 667 Mbit per second of photo traffic off the app servers.

india.title: KYC document uploads
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A lending app asks users to upload a PAN card photo and a selfie. The server returns presigned URLs to a private bucket with server-side encryption, scoped to keys like kyc/user-42/pan.jpg and valid for 5 minutes. After upload, a worker checks the file really is an image, runs it through OCR and face-match services, and records the result. Reviewers see the image only through short-lived presigned GET URLs, and every access is logged. A misconfigured public bucket of KYC documents is exactly the kind of breach that makes headlines, so 'private by default' is non-negotiable.

pitfalls.trap: Trusting the client's declared content type.
pitfalls.say: 'The presigned URL pins the content type and size limit, and a worker checks the real file signature before marking it ready, so a script renamed .jpg is rejected.'

pitfalls.trap: Uploading files through the API servers.
pitfalls.say: 'The server issues a presigned PUT URL and the client uploads straight to object storage; the server only stores metadata.'

pitfalls.trap: Making the bucket public for easy downloads.
pitfalls.say: 'The bucket stays private; downloads use short-lived presigned URLs or a CDN with origin access control.'

takeaways: Store blobs in object storage and metadata in the database.
Presigned URLs keep large payloads off app servers.
Validate and scan after upload, then mark ready.
Keep buckets private; serve through presigned URLs or a CDN.

client --1. request upload--> app (authz, metadata 'pending') --2. presigned URL--> client
client --3. PUT bytes--> object storage --4. event--> worker (scan, thumbnail) --> metadata 'ready'

title: HDFS
objectives: Describe the NameNode/DataNode split
Explain block replication and rack awareness
Know where HDFS fits and where it does not

cards.title: Big files, big blocks
cards.body: HDFS stores huge files split into large blocks (128 MB by default) across many DataNodes. One NameNode keeps the metadata: which blocks make up a file and where they live.

cards.title: Replication
cards.body: Each block is stored three times by default, with copies on different racks so a rack power failure does not lose data. Lost replicas are re-copied automatically.

mechanism.title: How HDFS writes and reads a file
steps: A file is split into large blocks, 128 MB by default. The NameNode keeps the namespace (directories, file-to-block mapping) in memory; DataNodes store the blocks on local disks.

To write, the client asks the NameNode for target DataNodes for each block. With replication factor 3 and rack awareness, the first replica goes on the writer's node (or a random one), the second on a node in a different rack, and the third on another node in that second rack.
The client streams the block to the first DataNode, which pipelines it to the second, which pipelines it to the third; acknowledgements flow back.
To read, the client asks the NameNode for block locations and reads each block from the closest replica, ideally on the same node, which is what lets MapReduce and Spark move computation to the data.
DataNodes send heartbeats and block reports; if one dies, the NameNode re-replicates its blocks from surviving copies.
The NameNode is critical, so production clusters run a standby NameNode with shared edit logs for high availability.

useWhen: Very large files written once and read in big sequential scans by batch jobs: logs, clickstreams, raw data for Spark.
On-premises big-data clusters where compute and storage sit on the same machines.
avoidWhen: Millions of tiny files: each file and block costs NameNode memory (roughly 150 bytes per object, a commonly cited estimate).
Low-latency random reads and in-place updates; HDFS files are append-only.

rows: Compute runs next to the data
Add nodes; NameNode memory limits files
Data lakes on S3 or GCS

numbers.title: Blocks and replication for a 1 TB file
steps: 1 TB is 1,048,576 MB in binary units; 1,048,576 ÷ 128 = 8,192 blocks.
Stored copies = 8,192 × 3 = 24,576 block replicas.
Raw disk used = 1 TB × 3 = 3 TB.
If the same data were 8 million files of 128 KB each, the NameNode would track at least 8 million file objects and 8 million block objects instead of 8,193, which is why small files hurt.
numbers.result: Large blocks keep NameNode metadata tiny; replication triples raw storage.

india.title: Telecom call records
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A large Indian telecom operator generates billions of call-detail and data-session records a day. Historically, operators processed such records on Hadoop clusters: hourly files of several gigabytes land in HDFS, replicated three times across racks, and nightly Spark jobs compute usage, fraud signals and network quality per tower. Each job reads big files sequentially from local disks, which HDFS does well. If the same records were written as one tiny file per call, the NameNode would run out of memory long before the disks filled. Many teams now keep the same layout on cloud object storage instead of HDFS.

pitfalls.trap: Storing millions of small images in HDFS.
pitfalls.say: 'HDFS metadata lives in NameNode memory, so small files hurt; I'd put images in object storage and use HDFS or a lake for large batch files.'

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting rack awareness.
pitfalls.say: 'Replicas span two racks so a rack switch failure does not lose all copies.'

takeaways: Files are split into 128 MB blocks, replicated 3 times across racks.
The NameNode holds all metadata in memory; small files are costly.
Reads go to the nearest replica, enabling data locality.
Best for large, write-once, sequentially read files.

NameNode: /logs/day1 -> [b1: DN1, DN4, DN5] [b2: DN2, DN6, DN7] ...
write pipeline: client -> DN1 (rack A) -> DN4 (rack B) -> DN5 (rack B)

mechanism.title: From document to search result in an inverted index
steps: Analysis at index time: the analyser lowercases text, splits it into tokens, removes stop words if configured, and stems or normalises words ('running' to 'run'). Custom analysers can add synonyms or n-grams for typos and partial matches.
Each term maps to a postings list: the document ids containing it, with positions and frequencies.

Query time: the query string is analysed the same way, the postings lists for its terms are fetched and intersected or merged, and documents are scored, typically with BM25 using term frequency, inverse document frequency and field length.
Elasticsearch splits an index into shards across nodes; each query fans out to the shards and the coordinating node merges the top results.
New documents become searchable after a refresh (by default every second), so search is near real-time, not instant.
The primary database stays the source of truth; changes flow to the index through events or CDC, and the index can be rebuilt from scratch.

useWhen: Full-text search, typo tolerance, relevance ranking, facets and filters over millions of documents.
Log search and analytics (the ELK stack) over large volumes of semi-structured text.
avoidWhen: Do not use Elasticsearch as the primary store for orders or payments; it is not transactional and can lose recent writes in some failures.
Do not use LIKE '%term%' over a large table for search; it cannot use a normal B-tree index and scans every row.

numbers.title: Why a LIKE scan is slow
assumptions: 10,000,000 product rows, 200 bytes of searchable text each
Disk or memory scan at 1 GB per second
steps: Text to scan = 10,000,000 × 200 bytes = 2,000,000,000 bytes, about 2 GB.
At 1 GB per second that is about 2 seconds per query, with all CPU cores busy.
An inverted index looks up the postings for 'paneer' directly, typically in milliseconds.
At 100 searches per second, LIKE would need about 200 seconds of scanning every second, which is impossible.
numbers.result: Substring scans grow with table size; an inverted index grows with the number of matching documents.

india.title: Searching a grocery catalogue
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A quick-commerce app in India must find 'paneer' when users type 'panner', 'paneer 200g' or 'पनीर'. Its search index uses an analyser with lowercasing, a synonym list (atta, wheat flour), n-grams or fuzzy matching for spelling mistakes, and a transliteration step for Hindi queries. Product data lives in Postgres; a CDC pipeline updates the Elasticsearch index within a second or two of a price or stock change. Results are filtered by the user's dark store and ranked by text match combined with popularity. If the index ever drifts, it is rebuilt from Postgres overnight.

pitfalls.trap: Treating the search index as the source of truth.
pitfalls.say: 'Postgres owns the data; the index is a derived copy updated by CDC and rebuilt if needed.'

pitfalls.trap: Using LIKE for search at scale.
pitfalls.say: 'LIKE with a leading wildcard scans every row; I'd use an inverted index with an analyser for typos and synonyms.'

takeaways: An inverted index maps terms to the documents containing them.
The same analyser must run at index and query time.
Search is near real-time (refresh about every second).
Keep the database as source of truth; sync the index by CDC or events.

index: paneer -> [3, 7, 19]   fresh -> [7, 11]
query 'panner' -> fuzzy -> paneer -> [3, 7, 19] -> score (BM25) -> top 10

cards.title: MapReduce
cards.body: Map: each worker reads a chunk and emits key-value pairs, such as (word, 1). Shuffle: pairs with the same key go to the same reducer. Reduce: combine the values per key. Moving computation to the data beats moving data.

cards.body: Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across steps instead of writing to disk after every MapReduce stage, so multi-step jobs and iterative ML run much faster. Lost partitions are recomputed from lineage.

cards.title: Shuffles are expensive
cards.body: The shuffle moves data across the network. A skewed key, such as one celebrity’s id, sends most data to one reducer, which runs for hours while the rest finish. Salt hot keys or pre-aggregate.

mechanism.title: How a MapReduce or Spark job runs
steps: Input is split into chunks (often one per storage block), and one map task per chunk runs on a node near the data.
Map: each task reads records and emits key-value pairs, for example (city, order_value) for every order.
Shuffle: pairs are partitioned by key (hash of city), written to local disk and pulled over the network so that all values for one key reach the same reducer. This is usually the most expensive step.
Reduce: each reducer aggregates the values for its keys, for example summing order values per city, and writes output files.

Spark generalises this into a graph (DAG) of stages, keeps intermediate data in memory where it fits, and recomputes lost partitions from lineage instead of writing every step to disk, which makes multi-step and iterative jobs much faster.

Skew: if one key has far more records (one huge city), its reducer runs long after the others finish. Fixes include salting the key into several sub-keys and combining afterwards, or broadcasting a small table instead of shuffling the big one.

useWhen: Large batch transformations and aggregations over data far bigger than one machine: daily reports, feature generation, backfills.
Spark for multi-step pipelines, iterative machine learning and SQL over a data lake.
avoidWhen: Interactive queries on small data; a single database or DuckDB is faster and simpler.
Real-time needs measured in seconds; use stream processing instead.

numbers.title: Effect of skew on job time
assumptions: 100 reducers; total work 10,000 reducer-seconds spread evenly would be 100 seconds each
One key (Mumbai) holds 20% of all records
steps: Even spread: each reducer does 10,000 ÷ 100 = 100 seconds of work.
The Mumbai reducer gets 20% of all work: 10,000 × 0.2 = 2,000 seconds.
The job finishes when the slowest reducer does, so about 2,000 seconds instead of 100, a 20× slowdown.
Salting Mumbai into 20 sub-keys gives each about 100 seconds, then a tiny second step adds the 20 partial sums.
numbers.result: One hot key can make a job 20 times slower; salting spreads it across reducers.

india.title: Daily settlement reports
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A payments aggregator in India computes daily settlement files for lakhs of merchants: total captured, refunds, fees and GST per merchant. A Spark job reads the day's transaction files from the data lake, maps each transaction to (merchant_id, amounts), shuffles by merchant and sums. A handful of very large merchants produce a large share of transactions, so the job salts their ids to spread the work, then combines the partial sums. The output feeds settlement and reconciliation, and because it is batch, a rerun after a bug fix simply recomputes the day from immutable input.

pitfalls.trap: Using Spark for a query over 2 GB.
pitfalls.say: 'Two gigabytes fits on one machine; Postgres or DuckDB answers faster without cluster overhead.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring skew.
pitfalls.say: 'Merchant volume is skewed, so I'd salt the biggest merchant keys or broadcast the small dimension table to avoid one slow reducer.'

takeaways: Map emits key-value pairs; shuffle groups by key; reduce aggregates.
The shuffle is usually the most expensive step.
Spark keeps intermediates in memory and recovers via lineage.
Skewed keys dominate job time; salt them.

input splits -> map (merchant, amt) -> shuffle by key -> reduce (sum per merchant) -> output
 hot key 'M1' -> salt: M1#0..M1#19 -> partial sums -> combine

cards.body: Streams are unbounded, so you aggregate over windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) or session (gaps of inactivity). Use event time, when it happened, not processing time, when it arrived.

mechanism.title: How a stream processor computes a windowed count
steps: Events (clicks, payments, rider pings) arrive continuously from a log such as Kafka, partitioned by key.
The processor (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) reads each partition and keeps state per key, for example counts per merchant, in a local store that is checkpointed regularly.
Windows group events in time: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping 1-minute buckets), sliding or hopping (5-minute windows every minute) and session windows (closed after a gap of inactivity).
Event time is when the event happened; processing time is when it is processed. Mobile events can arrive minutes late, so correct results use event time.

Watermarks estimate how far event time has progressed ('no more events older than 12:04:30 expected'). When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window is emitted; later stragglers go to a side output or update the result.
On failure, the job restarts from the last checkpoint and replays input from the matching offsets; with transactional sinks or idempotent writes, results are exactly-once in effect.

useWhen: Fraud detection, live dashboards, alerting, surge pricing and anything that must react within seconds.
Continuous ETL that keeps search indexes, caches or warehouses fresh.
avoidWhen: Jobs where hourly or daily results are fine; batch is simpler and cheaper.
Complex joins over months of history; precompute those in batch and join the stream to the result.

numbers.title: State size for per-user 5-minute windows
assumptions: Sliding window of 5 minutes, advancing every minute, so each event belongs to 5 windows
State per user per window about 100 bytes
steps: Windows open per user at any time = 5.
State = 2,000,000 × 5 = 10,000,000 window entries.
Memory = 10,000,000 × 100 bytes = 1,000,000,000 bytes, about 1 GB, spread across the job's parallel tasks.
A 60-minute sliding window advancing every minute would need 12 times as much, about 12 GB.
numbers.result: Window length divided by slide sets how many windows each key keeps; size state before choosing windows.

india.title: Card-fraud checks on UPI and cards
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A payments processor wants to flag a card used in Delhi and then in Chennai within ten minutes, or more than five failed attempts in a minute. A stream job keyed by card or VPA keeps recent locations and failure counts in state, using event time from the terminal or app so that delayed events from patchy networks still land in the right window. The watermark allows, say, 30 seconds of lateness; events arriving later are routed to a side output for review rather than silently dropped. Decisions flow back within a second or two, quickly enough to step up authentication on the next attempt.

pitfalls.trap: Treating late events as impossible.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd set an allowed lateness, route anything later to a side output, and monitor how many events arrive late so the watermark can be tuned.'

pitfalls.trap: Windowing by processing time for mobile events.
pitfalls.say: 'Mobile events arrive late, so I'd window by event time with watermarks and a lateness allowance.'

pitfalls.trap: Assuming the stream never replays.
pitfalls.say: 'After a failure the job replays from the checkpoint, so sinks are idempotent or transactional.'

takeaways: Streams give second-level latency with always-on state.
Use event time and watermarks for correct windows.
Window size divided by slide multiplies state.
Checkpoints plus replay need idempotent or transactional sinks.

mechanism.title: From production database to dashboard
steps: OLTP databases serve the app: many small reads and writes by key, row-oriented storage, strict transactions.
Extract: copy changes out of OLTP, by nightly dumps or, better, CDC streaming.
Land raw data cheaply in a data lake (files such as Parquet on object storage).

Transform: clean, deduplicate, join and model into fact tables (orders, payments) and dimension tables (customers, cities, products). With ELT the transformation runs inside the warehouse using SQL tools such as dbt.

Load into a columnar warehouse or OLAP engine (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse). Columnar storage reads only the columns a query touches and compresses them well, so scans of billions of rows are fast.
Dashboards and analysts query the warehouse, never the production primary.
Partition big fact tables by date and cluster them by common filters such as city, so a query for one week reads only that week's files instead of the whole history.

useWhen: Warehouse or OLAP for aggregates over large history: revenue by city and month, cohort retention, funnels.
A lakehouse (open table formats such as Iceberg or Delta on object storage) when many engines must read the same data cheaply.
avoidWhen: Do not run heavy analytical queries on the OLTP primary; full scans evict hot pages and slow the app.
Do not use a warehouse to serve per-user app requests at thousands per second; it is built for scans, not point lookups.

rows: Small, by key, many per second

numbers.title: Why columnar scans are cheaper
assumptions: 1,000,000,000 order rows, 40 columns of 8 bytes each
Query sums one column grouped by one other column
steps: Row store reads every column: 1,000,000,000 × 320 bytes = 320,000,000,000 bytes, about 320 GB.
Column store reads 2 columns: 1,000,000,000 × 16 bytes = 16,000,000,000 bytes, about 16 GB.
With typical 5× compression on columnar data, that is about 3.2 GB.
So the same query reads roughly 100 times less data.
numbers.result: Reading only the needed columns, compressed, is why warehouses scan billions of rows in seconds.

india.title: City-wise sales for a festive season
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian retail chain wants Diwali-week revenue by city, category and payment method, compared with last year. Running that on the order database during the sale would scan years of orders and slow checkouts. Instead, CDC streams orders into a lake every few minutes, dbt models build an orders fact table with city and product dimensions, and the warehouse answers the query over hundreds of millions of rows in seconds. The finance team accepts data that is 15 minutes old, and the checkout database never sees an analytical query.

pitfalls.trap: Assuming the warehouse is real time.
pitfalls.say: 'CDC into the warehouse gives minutes of delay; for a live operations screen I'd use a stream processor or an OLAP engine like ClickHouse fed from Kafka.'

pitfalls.trap: Running reports on the production primary.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd stream changes via CDC into a warehouse; dashboards query that, so the OLTP database only serves the app.'

pitfalls.trap: Serving app traffic from the warehouse.
pitfalls.say: 'The warehouse is for scans; precomputed results needed by the app are exported to a cache or key-value store.'

takeaways: OLTP serves the app; OLAP serves analysis.
Columnar storage reads only needed columns and compresses well.
Use CDC and ELT to feed the warehouse without loading production.
Model analytics as facts and dimensions.

Answer “nearby” queries without scanning every row
Handle cell boundaries and dense cities

cards.title: Nearby without a full scan
cards.body: Computing distance to every restaurant in India per request is too slow. Geospatial indexes bucket locations into cells so a query only checks nearby cells.

cards.title: Geohash and quadtrees
cards.body: Geohash encodes lat/long into a string; a shared prefix means nearby. Quadtrees split space into four until each cell holds few points, so dense Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas get big ones.

steps: Get user’s geohash cell
Add the 8 neighbouring cells

Compute exact distance and sort

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Searching only the user’s own cell. A restaurant 50 m away can sit across a cell boundary, so always include neighbouring cells.

choices.label: A restaurant 50 m away can sit just across the boundary

questions.explanation: Cells are arbitrary lines on the map.

choices.label: Cells split where points are dense, so Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas big ones

questions.explanation: Adaptive cells keep candidate counts even.

questions.prompt: Order a “nearby within 2 km” query.
questions.explanation: Coarse filter, then exact check.

choices.label: They are in the same country only
One is north of the other

questions.explanation: A shared prefix means a shared cell.

Dense cities get finer cells
Scanning every restaurant is fine on fast CPUs

Because geohashes only work in groups of nine
