mechanism.title: Finding nearby drivers with geohashes
steps: A geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a string by repeatedly halving the world, interleaving longitude and latitude bits, and writing them in base 32. Each extra character narrows the cell.
Points in the same cell share a prefix, so a prefix lookup in a sorted index or a hash map finds them quickly.
Precision examples (approximate): 5 characters is about 4.9 km by 4.9 km; 6 characters about 1.2 km by 0.6 km; 7 characters about 153 m by 153 m.
To search 'within 2 km', choose a precision whose cells are about the radius, look up the user's cell and its 8 neighbours, because a nearby driver may sit just across a cell edge.
Filter candidates by exact distance (haversine) and rank by distance or estimated arrival time.
Alternatives: quadtrees split dense areas into smaller cells adaptively; Google's S2 and Uber's H3 use hierarchical cells (H3 uses hexagons, which have uniform neighbour distances).

useWhen: Nearby search for drivers, restaurants, stores, and geofencing such as 'is this rider inside the delivery zone'.
Geohash or H3 keys in Redis, Elasticsearch or a key-value store; PostGIS for rich polygon queries.
avoidWhen: Do not scan all drivers and compute distances one by one; it grows linearly with fleet size.
Do not search only the user's own cell; nearby points across the edge are missed.

rows: Simple prefix search in any store

numbers.title: Why the 9-cell lookup is cheap
assumptions: 50,000 active drivers in a city of about 1,500 square km
Search with 6-character geohash cells of about 1.2 km × 0.6 km (0.72 square km)
steps: Driver density = 50,000 ÷ 1,500 ≈ 33 drivers per square km on average.
Nine cells cover 9 × 0.72 = 6.48 square km.
Expected candidates = 33 × 6.48 ≈ 214 drivers, instead of 50,000.
Computing 214 exact distances takes microseconds; dense areas may need finer cells or a cap on candidates.
numbers.result: The 9-cell geohash lookup cuts the candidates from 50,000 to about 200 before exact distance checks.

india.title: Auto-rickshaw matching in Bengaluru
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A ride-hailing app receives location pings from auto drivers every few seconds. Each ping updates the driver's cell key (a geohash or H3 index) in an in-memory store. When a rider in Koramangala requests a ride, the dispatcher reads the rider's cell and its neighbours, filters by vehicle type and availability, and ranks by estimated arrival time using road distance rather than straight-line distance, since a flyover or one-way street can make a near driver slow to arrive. In dense areas at peak time, the dispatcher uses finer cells to keep candidate lists short.

pitfalls.trap: Searching only the rider's cell.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd search the cell plus its 8 neighbours, then filter by exact distance, because the nearest driver may be across a cell boundary.'

pitfalls.trap: Ranking by straight-line distance.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd shortlist by distance, then rank by estimated arrival time from a routing service.'

takeaways: Geohashes turn 2D proximity into string prefixes.
Pick a precision near the search radius and include the 8 neighbours.
Filter candidates by exact distance, rank by ETA.
Quadtrees and H3 adapt better to density and geometry.

title: Time-Series DBs
objectives: Recognise time-series workloads
Explain downsampling and retention
Avoid high-cardinality labels

cards.title: Append-heavy, time-ordered
cards.body: Metrics, sensor readings and prices arrive as timestamped points, mostly appended and read as ranges (last hour, last week). Time-series databases compress and index for exactly that.

cards.title: Retention and rollups
cards.body: Raw 10-second points for 7 days, 1-minute averages for 90 days, hourly for years. Downsampling keeps dashboards fast and storage bounded.

cards.title: A metric’s life
cards.body: 5 steps from “Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}” to “Raw data expires after retention”, via “Ingest appends to the current time block”.
steps: Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}
Ingest appends to the current time block
Compaction compresses old blocks
Rollup job writes 1-minute averages
Raw data expires after retention

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Putting user IDs or request IDs in labels. Every unique label combination is a new series, so cardinality explodes and memory with it.

questions.prompt: Metrics memory jumped 50× after a deploy that added a user_id label. Why?

choices.label: user_id values are stored as long strings
Each user id creates a new series, so the series count explodes
The database cannot index numeric labels

questions.explanation: Every label combination is a series.

questions.prompt: Dashboards over a year of 10-second data are slow and storage keeps growing. What helps most?

choices.label: Downsample older data and set retention
Move metrics into a relational database
Keep raw data forever on faster disks

questions.explanation: Rollups keep old data cheap to query.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most time-series shaped?

choices.label: CPU usage from 5,000 servers every 10 seconds

questions.explanation: Timestamped, append-heavy, read as ranges.

questions.prompt: Order a metric’s life.

items.label: Ingest appends it to the current block

questions.explanation: Raw data is short-lived; rollups last.

questions.prompt: 5,000 hosts each report 50 metrics every 10 s. How many points per second are ingested?
questions.workedAnswer: 5,000 × 50 = 250,000 series; one point per 10 s gives 25,000 points/s.
questions.explanation: 5,000 × 50 = 250,000 series; one point per 10 s gives 25,000 points/s.

questions.prompt: Labels have 20, 25, 5 and 10 possible values. How many series can the metric create?
questions.explanation: Series multiply across labels: 20 × 25 = 500, 500 × 5 = 2,500 and 2,500 × 10 = 25,000.

Unbounded label values such as user or request IDs.
A range scan over a time window for a series.

mechanism.title: How a time-series database stores and ages data
steps: Each series is identified by a metric name plus labels, such as http_requests_total{service='checkout', status='500'}. Each sample is a timestamp and a value.
Incoming samples are appended to the current time block in memory and to a write-ahead log, then compressed into immutable blocks (for example 2 hours in Prometheus).
Compression exploits regularity: timestamps are delta-of-delta encoded and values XOR-encoded (the Gorilla technique), which brings typical samples down to roughly 1–2 bytes.
Queries select series by labels and aggregate over time ranges: rate over 5 minutes, p99 over an hour.
Retention and rollups: keep raw 15-second samples for, say, 15 days, 5-minute rollups for 90 days and 1-hour rollups for years, deleting whole old blocks cheaply.
Cardinality, the number of unique label combinations, drives memory and index size; a label such as user_id or order_id can explode it into millions of series.

useWhen: Metrics, IoT sensor readings, prices and other append-mostly, time-stamped numeric data queried by time range.
Prometheus for monitoring; TimescaleDB, InfluxDB or ClickHouse for longer-term or richer time-series analytics.
avoidWhen: Do not store per-event business records (orders, payments) as metrics; they belong in a database or logs.
Do not use unbounded labels such as user id, request id or full URL.

rows: Bounded disk, long history at low resolution

numbers.title: Cardinality and storage
assumptions: Metric with labels service (20), endpoint (25), status (5), instance (10)
Scrape every 15 s, about 1.5 bytes per compressed sample
steps: Samples per series per day = 86,400 ÷ 15 = 5,760.
Samples per day = 25,000 × 5,760 = 144,000,000, so about 216 MB per day compressed.
Adding a user_id label with 1,000,000 values would multiply series by up to a million, which no monitoring setup can hold.
numbers.result: Labels multiply series counts; a few bounded labels are cheap, one unbounded label is fatal.

india.title: Monitoring a payments switch on festival days
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During peak days such as Diwali, UPI volumes are publicly reported to hit records. A bank's payment team watches success rate, latency and error codes per partner bank and per API in Prometheus and Grafana, with labels kept to bounded sets such as partner bank, API and response code. Raw 15-second data shows exactly when a partner bank started timing out; hourly rollups kept for two years let the team compare this Diwali with the last two. Investigating one customer's failed payment uses logs and traces keyed by transaction id, not a metric label.

pitfalls.trap: Alerting on raw per-instance metrics with no aggregation.
pitfalls.say: 'I alert on aggregated SLO signals such as checkout error rate across instances, and use per-instance series only to drill down.'

pitfalls.trap: Adding user_id as a metric label to debug one customer.
pitfalls.say: 'Per-user detail goes in logs and traces; metric labels stay bounded, such as service, endpoint and status.'

pitfalls.trap: Keeping raw samples forever.
pitfalls.say: 'Raw data for 15 days, then 5-minute and hourly rollups, so storage stays bounded.'

takeaways: Time-series stores append, compress and query by time range.
Cardinality, not sample count, is the usual scaling limit.
Retention plus rollups keep long history affordable.
Per-entity detail belongs in logs and traces, not labels.

series = name + labels  -> [t1,v1][t2,v2]... (delta-of-delta + XOR, ~1.5 bytes/sample)
raw 15 s (15 d) -> 5 min rollup (90 d) -> 1 h rollup (2 y)

title: Blue-Green/Canary/Feature Flags
objectives: Compare blue-green and canary releases
Use feature flags and kill switches safely
Keep schema changes rollback-safe

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.body: Run two full environments. Deploy to the idle one (green), test it, then switch the router from blue to green. Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the switch, and database changes must work for both.

cards.title: Canary
cards.body: Send a small share of traffic (1%, then 5%, 25%) to the new version and watch error rates and latency. Roll back automatically if they get worse. It catches problems only real traffic shows.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.body: Ship code dark and turn features on per user, region or percentage at runtime. Kill switches turn a broken feature off without a deploy. Remove flags once rolled out, or they pile up as untested paths.

cards.title: A canary rollout
cards.body: 5 steps from “Deploy v2 next to v1” to “Roll back if metrics worsen”, via “Route 1% of traffic to v2”.
steps: Deploy v2 next to v1
Route 1% of traffic to v2
Compare errors and latency
Increase to 25%, then 100%
Roll back if metrics worsen

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Shipping a schema change the old version cannot read, then rolling back. Make changes backward compatible: add the new column, switch code, remove the old column later.

questions.prompt: What does a canary release do?

choices.label: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate
Switches all traffic at once and rolls back if users complain
Deploys to every server at 2 AM

questions.explanation: Real traffic, limited blast radius.

questions.prompt: In blue-green, how do you roll back?

choices.label: Redeploy the old build to every server
Point the router back to the old environment

questions.explanation: The old environment is still running.

questions.prompt: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?

choices.label: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag

questions.explanation: Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

questions.prompt: Order a canary rollout.
questions.explanation: Grow only while metrics hold.

questions.prompt: Order a rollback-safe column rename.

items.label: Switch reads to the new column

questions.explanation: Every step works with the previous code version.

questions.prompt: Why use expand-and-contract for a column rename during a canary?

choices.label: Old and new code versions run at the same time and both must work with the schema
So feature flags are not needed

questions.explanation: During a gradual rollout both versions are live, so schema changes must stay compatible with both.

flashcards.front: What does a canary release do?
flashcards.back: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate. Real traffic, limited blast radius.

flashcards.front: In blue-green, how do you roll back?
flashcards.back: Point the router back to the old environment. The old environment is still running.

flashcards.front: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?
flashcards.back: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag. Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How a canary release with flags rolls out
steps: Blue-green: run the new version (green) alongside the old (blue) on full capacity, test it, then switch all traffic at the load balancer. Rollback is switching back.
Canary: send a small share of real traffic (say 1%) to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old, and step up through 5%, 25%, 50% and 100% if healthy.
Automated analysis checks the canary against guardrail metrics and rolls back on a breach without waiting for a human.
Feature flags separate deploy from release: code ships dark, and the feature is turned on per user, per city or per percentage, and off instantly if it misbehaves.
Database changes use expand and contract: add the new column or table first (compatible with old code), deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only later drop the old column.
Clean up flags after rollout; stale flags become hidden complexity.

useWhen: Canary for risky changes to high-traffic services where real traffic reveals problems tests miss.
Feature flags for gradual product launches, A/B tests and kill switches for risky features.
avoidWhen: Blue-green for stateful systems where both versions cannot safely share the database schema.
Long-lived flags for permanent configuration; they are for rollouts, not settings.

numbers.title: How many users a canary exposes
assumptions: A bug fails 20% of requests on the new version
steps: Canary traffic = 1,000,000 × 0.01 = 10,000 requests per hour, so about 5,000 in 30 minutes.
Failed requests = 5,000 × 0.2 = 1,000.
A big-bang deploy with the same bug for the same 30 minutes would fail 500,000 × 0.2 = 100,000 requests.
With automated rollback after 5 minutes instead of 30, failures drop to about 167.
numbers.result: A 1% canary with fast automated rollback limits a bad release to hundreds of failures instead of a hundred thousand.

india.title: Launching a new checkout in one city
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A food-delivery app redesigns its checkout. The code ships to all servers behind a flag that is off. The team turns it on for employees, then for 1% of users in Jaipur, watching payment success rate and order completion against the old flow. Payment success drops slightly for one bank's netbanking users, so they turn the flag off for that segment within minutes, fix it, and resume. Over two weeks the flag goes to 100% across cities, and the old code and the flag are deleted. No deploy was ever rolled back; only flags moved.

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll deploy on Friday night when traffic is low and fix bugs Monday.'
pitfalls.say: 'I'd canary at 1% with automated rollback on error and latency guardrails, during working hours when the team can respond.'

pitfalls.trap: Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd expand and contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release.'

takeaways: Separate deploy from release with feature flags.
Canaries limit blast radius; automate rollback on guardrails.
Blue-green gives instant switch-back but needs double capacity.
Use expand and contract for schema changes.

deploy v2 dark --> flag on: staff --> 1% --> 5% --> 25% --> 100% --> delete flag

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what a container packages
Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals
Use readiness vs liveness probes correctly

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: 5 steps from “New image pushed” to “One old pod is removed, repeat”, via “Deployment creates a new pod”.
steps: New image pushed
Deployment creates a new pod
Readiness probe passes
Service starts sending traffic
One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: The database blips and every pod restarts in a loop. What is misconfigured?

choices.label: The readiness probe checks the database
The rolling update is too fast
The liveness probe checks the database

questions.explanation: Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: A node running three checkout pods dies. What does Kubernetes do?

choices.label: Schedules replacement pods on healthy nodes
Waits for the node to come back

questions.explanation: Controllers restore the declared state.

questions.prompt: Order one step of a rolling deploy.
questions.explanation: Old pods leave only after new ones are ready.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start in seconds while a VM takes minutes?

choices.label: Containers only run on bare metal
It shares the host kernel instead of booting its own OS

questions.explanation: No guest OS boot.

questions.prompt: You declared 5 replicas of checkout and one crashes. What happens?

choices.label: Nothing until you run kubectl again
Kubernetes sees 4 running instead of 5 and starts a new pod

questions.explanation: Reconciliation loops close the gap.

questions.prompt: A pod is still loading its cache and should not get traffic yet. Which probe handles this?
questions.explanation: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether to restart it.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and start in seconds.
Failing it removes the pod from traffic without restarting it.
Failing it restarts the container.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How Kubernetes keeps an app running
steps: A container image packages the app and its dependencies; it runs as an isolated process using Linux namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel.
You declare desired state in a Deployment: image version, 6 replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits, probes.

The scheduler places pods on nodes with enough free requested resources; controllers continuously compare actual state with desired state and fix differences, for example restarting a crashed pod or replacing pods from a failed node.
Probes: the liveness probe restarts a stuck container; the readiness probe controls whether the pod receives traffic; the startup probe gives slow starters time before liveness kicks in.
Rolling update: change the image tag; Kubernetes creates new pods and removes old ones gradually, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, sending traffic only to ready pods.
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts the replica count from metrics such as CPU utilisation against the requested CPU.

useWhen: Many services needing consistent deploys, autoscaling, self-healing and service discovery.
Teams with the skills (or a managed offering such as EKS, GKE or AKS) to operate it.
avoidWhen: A single small app where a managed platform (a PaaS or serverless) is simpler and cheaper.
Do not use the liveness probe to check downstream dependencies; a database blip would restart every pod at once.

numbers.title: Sizing replicas and a rolling update
assumptions: Peak 3,000 requests per second; one pod handles 250 at target CPU
Rolling update with maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 0
steps: Pods needed at peak = 3,000 ÷ 250 = 12.
Add N+2 headroom for a node failure and deploys: 14 replicas.
maxSurge 25% of 14 is 3.5, rounded up to 4 extra pods during the rollout; maxUnavailable 0 keeps all 14 serving.
So the cluster needs room for 14 plus 4 = 18 pods' worth of requested resources during deploys.
numbers.result: Size replicas from peak load per pod plus headroom, and reserve surge capacity so rolling updates never reduce serving pods.

india.title: Exam-results day for an ed-tech app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When board exam results are published, an ed-tech app's result-lookup service can see traffic jump many times over within minutes. On Kubernetes, the team pre-scales the Deployment the night before, sets a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a higher ceiling, and makes sure the cluster autoscaler can add nodes. Readiness probes keep new pods out of rotation until they have loaded the cache of school codes. When one node fails under load, the controller reschedules its pods elsewhere within a minute, and students only see slightly slower responses.

pitfalls.trap: Liveness probes that check the database.
pitfalls.say: 'Liveness checks only that the process can respond; dependency health goes in readiness or metrics, so a database blip does not restart every pod.'

pitfalls.trap: Setting CPU limits far below what a JVM or Node process needs at peak.
pitfalls.say: 'I set requests from measured usage and leave headroom on limits, because CPU throttling shows up as latency spikes that are hard to diagnose.'

pitfalls.trap: No resource requests.
pitfalls.say: 'Pods get CPU and memory requests so the scheduler can place them and the autoscaler has a baseline.'

takeaways: Containers package apps; Kubernetes reconciles desired state.
Readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup protects slow boots.
Rolling updates are bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
Size replicas from per-pod throughput plus headroom.

title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination
objectives: Explain why deep offsets are slow
Implement cursor pagination with a stable key
Pick offset or cursor for a given screen

cards.title: Offset pagination
cards.body: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 is simple and lets users jump to page 500, but the database still walks past 10,000 rows, and inserts shift pages so items repeat or vanish.

cards.title: Cursor pagination
cards.body: Return an opaque cursor (the last item’s sort key) and fetch WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor LIMIT 20. Each page is an index seek, and new inserts do not shift what comes next. There is no jumping to page 500.

cards.title: Paging a feed with cursors
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client asks for the first 20” to “Repeat until there is no cursor”, via “Server returns items and next_cursor”.
steps: Client asks for the first 20
Server returns items and next_cursor
Client sends next_cursor
Server seeks past it using the index
Repeat until there is no cursor

cards.title: A stable sort key
cards.body: Cursors need a unique, ordered key. created_at alone can tie, so use (created_at, id), with an index on that pair.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed. Deep pages get slower and new posts push items onto the next page, so users see duplicates.

questions.prompt: Why is OFFSET 100000 slow?

choices.label: The database still reads and discards 100,000 rows

questions.explanation: Offsets are skipped, not jumped over.

questions.prompt: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?

choices.label: The new posts appended at the bottom
Duplicates, as earlier items shift onto the next page

questions.explanation: Inserts move everything down.

questions.prompt: Which cursor key is safe?
questions.explanation: Unique and ordered.

questions.prompt: Order cursor paging.
questions.explanation: Each page starts from the last one seen.

questions.prompt: Pagination for an admin table of 5,000 rows where staff jump to arbitrary pages.

rationaleOptions.label: Cursors let staff jump straight to page 37
Offset supports jumping to any page
At 5,000 rows the skipped rows cost little

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cursors only move forward from a known position.

questions.explanation: Small, stable tables with page jumps suit offsets.

questions.prompt: Why is (created_at, id) used as the cursor instead of created_at alone?

choices.label: Many rows can share a timestamp, so the id breaks ties and prevents skipped or repeated rows

questions.explanation: The sort key must be unique; adding the id makes the order total.

flashcards.back: The database still reads and discards 100,000 rows. Offsets are skipped, not jumped over.

flashcards.front: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?
flashcards.back: Duplicates, as earlier items shift onto the next page. Inserts move everything down.
(created_at, id). Unique and ordered.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How offset and cursor pagination execute
steps: Offset: SELECT ... ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. The database must walk and discard 10,000 rows before returning 20, so later pages get slower.
Offset is also unstable: if new rows are inserted while the user scrolls, items shift between pages, causing duplicates or gaps.

Cursor (keyset): return the sort key of the last item as an opaque cursor. The next query asks for rows strictly after it: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20.
With an index on (created_at, id), the database seeks directly to the cursor position and reads 20 entries, so every page costs about the same.
The sort key must be unique and stable; add the id as a tie-breaker because many rows can share a timestamp.
Encode the cursor (for example base64 of the values) so clients treat it as opaque and you can change its format later.

useWhen: Cursor pagination for infinite scroll, feeds, chat history, API list endpoints and large tables.
Offset pagination for small admin tables where users jump to page 7 and data rarely changes.
avoidWhen: Do not use deep offsets on large tables; page 5,000 scans 100,000 rows to show 20.
Do not build a cursor on a non-unique column alone; ties cause skipped or repeated rows.

rows: Unique sort key and matching index

numbers.title: Rows touched by deep pages
steps: Offset skips (5,000 − 1) × 20 = 99,980 rows, then reads 20, so about 100,000 rows touched.
Cursor seeks once in the index (a few page reads for a B-tree) and reads 20 rows.
At 200 such requests per second, offset touches about 200 × 100,000 = 20,000,000 rows per second; the cursor touches about 4,000.
That gap is the difference between a struggling database and an idle one.
numbers.result: Offset cost grows linearly with page depth; cursor cost stays at one index seek plus the page.

india.title: Scrolling a long transaction history
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A user of a UPI app scrolls back through two years of payments, perhaps thousands of entries. With offset pagination, each 'load more' asks the database to skip more and more rows, and if a new payment arrives mid-scroll, one entry shifts and appears twice. With a cursor of (transaction_time, transaction_id), each request seeks directly to where the last page ended using the index and returns the next 20, and a new payment at the top does not disturb older pages. The app sends the opaque cursor string it received; it never computes page numbers.

pitfalls.trap: Exposing raw database ids and timestamps as the cursor format.
pitfalls.say: 'The cursor is an opaque, encoded string, so clients cannot tamper with its meaning and I can change the sort key later without breaking them.'

pitfalls.trap: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed.

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention

mechanism.title: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking in practice
steps: Pessimistic: read the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction. Other writers (and other FOR UPDATE readers) wait until you commit, so your read-modify-write is safe.
Optimistic: read the row and its version number without locking. When writing, run UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?.
If the update affects 1 row, you won. If it affects 0 rows, someone else changed it first: re-read, reapply the change, and retry or report a conflict.
Under low contention, optimistic locking avoids holding locks while users think or while the app does other work.
Under high contention, optimistic locking wastes work on retries, while pessimistic locks queue writers in order.
Keep lock scope small either way: lock one row, not a table; hold locks for milliseconds, never across a user's think time or an external API call.

useWhen: Optimistic for edits that rarely collide: profile updates, document metadata, admin forms (and HTTP ETag with If-Match).
Pessimistic (or a single conditional update) for hot rows such as inventory counts or seat holds during a flash sale.
avoidWhen: Optimistic retries on a hot counter where most attempts conflict; throughput collapses.
Pessimistic locks held across user interaction, such as while a checkout form is open.

numbers.title: Retries under contention
assumptions: Each attempt succeeds with probability p (no one else wrote in between)
Case A: p = 0.95; case B: p = 0.2
steps: Expected attempts = 1 ÷ p.
Case A: 1 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 1.05 attempts, so retries are almost free.
Case B: 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 attempts on average, each doing the read and computation again.
At case B contention, a pessimistic lock or one atomic conditional UPDATE is cheaper.
numbers.result: Optimistic locking costs 1 ÷ p attempts; it shines when conflicts are rare and hurts on hot rows.

india.title: Editing a restaurant menu versus selling the last biryani
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Two managers of a restaurant on a delivery platform edit the same menu item from different laptops. Conflicts are rare, so the item carries a version number; if the second save finds the version changed, the app shows 'this item was updated by someone else, review changes'. Meanwhile, during dinner rush, the 'portions left' counter for a popular biryani is updated by many orders at once. Here the platform avoids read-modify-write entirely with UPDATE items SET left = left − 1 WHERE id = ? AND left > 0, which the database serialises on that row and which never oversells.

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting deadlocks with pessimistic locks.
pitfalls.say: 'Every transaction locks rows in the same order, such as by ascending id, and has a lock timeout, so two transactions cannot wait on each other forever.'

pitfalls.trap: Using optimistic locking for a flash-sale counter.

pitfalls.trap: Holding a lock while waiting for the payment gateway.

takeaways: Optimistic checks a version at write time; pessimistic blocks others.
Expected optimistic attempts are 1 ÷ p.
Use atomic conditional updates for hot counters.
Never hold locks across user think time or external calls.

mechanism.title: How OT and CRDTs merge concurrent edits
steps: Problem: two users edit the same document at once. Alice inserts 'X' at position 0 while Bob deletes the character at position 3. Applying each other's operations naively shifts positions and corrupts the text.

Operational transformation (OT): operations go through a central server that orders them. When Bob's delete arrives after Alice's insert, the server transforms it (position 3 becomes 4) so it still deletes the intended character.
OT needs carefully proven transformation functions for every pair of operation types and is easiest with a central server, which is the approach Google Docs is publicly known to use.

CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) give every character a unique, ordered id (for example based on site id and counter), so inserts and deletes refer to ids, not positions, and replicas can apply operations in any order and still converge.
CRDTs work peer-to-peer and offline, at the cost of metadata per character and tombstones for deletions, which need compaction.
Last-writer-wins on the whole document is not collaborative editing: one user's changes silently disappear.

useWhen: OT for server-centred real-time editors where a central service orders all operations.
CRDTs for offline-first and peer-to-peer apps, and for structured data such as counters, sets and maps (libraries such as Yjs and Automerge).
avoidWhen: Do not use last-writer-wins for documents edited concurrently.
Do not implement OT transformation functions from scratch unless you must; they are notoriously easy to get wrong.

numbers.title: Metadata cost of a text CRDT
assumptions: About 16 bytes of id and ordering metadata per character (illustrative)
Another 20,000 deleted characters kept as tombstones
steps: Live characters: 50,000 × 16 bytes = 800,000 bytes, about 0.8 MB of metadata.
Tombstones: 20,000 × 16 bytes = 320,000 bytes.
Total metadata is about 1.12 MB for 50 KB of text, more than 20 times the text itself.
Libraries reduce this with run-length encoding of consecutive inserts and periodic garbage collection.
numbers.result: CRDT convergence is paid for in metadata, so production libraries compress runs and collect tombstones.

india.title: Co-editing a project report
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Three engineering students in Pune edit a project report together: two online in a browser editor, one on a train with patchy network. In a server-centred editor using OT, each keystroke travels to the server, which orders and transforms it, so the offline student cannot edit meaningfully until reconnected. In a CRDT-based editor, the offline student keeps typing, and when the train reaches a station with signal, their changes merge with the others' without conflicts or lost paragraphs. Whole-file last-writer-wins, the behaviour of naive file sync, would keep only the last person's save.

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring tombstone growth in a CRDT.
pitfalls.say: 'Deleted elements stay as tombstones, so I'd rely on a library that compacts them and snapshot documents periodically.'

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll lock the document while someone edits.'
pitfalls.say: 'Real-time editors merge concurrent edits; I'd use OT with a central server or a CRDT library such as Yjs if offline editing matters.'

pitfalls.trap: Proposing last-writer-wins for documents.
pitfalls.say: 'LWW drops a user's edits silently; text needs OT or a sequence CRDT.'

takeaways: Positions shift under concurrent edits; merging needs OT or CRDTs.
OT transforms operations through a central server.
CRDTs use unique ids so replicas converge in any order, even offline.
Last-writer-wins on documents loses work.

steps: POST /v1/pastes stores the text in object storage under a random key and writes metadata (id, owner, size, visibility, expires_at) in SQL.
Ids are random base62 strings of 8 or more characters so private pastes cannot be guessed by enumeration.
GET /p/{id} reads metadata (cached in Redis), checks visibility and expiry, then streams content from object storage or a CDN for public pastes.
A scheduled job deletes expired pastes in batches using an index on expires_at; object storage lifecycle rules can also expire objects by prefix.
Large pastes are capped (for example 10 MB) and syntax highlighting is done on the client.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 77 · Rate Limiter: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server. In scope: Limit requests per user/IP/key; Return 429 with retry hint; Configurable rules.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 77 non-functionals: Adds < 5 ms latency. Highly available. Shared across instances. Out of scope: Billing and quota invoicing; Bot detection with ML.

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 77 risks: Fail open or fail closed?: Failing closed during a Redis outage blocks every login; failing open lets attackers through. Choosing keys: Indian mobile carriers put many users behind shared IPs, so per-phone and per-user limits are primary and IP limits are loose, catching only obvious floods.

questions.prompt: A client gets 429 and immediately retries in a tight loop. What should the response tell it?

choices.label: A 500 error so the client treats it as a server fault
Nothing; silently drop the connection to save work
A 200 with an empty body so the client stops retrying
A Retry-After header with when the bucket refills

questions.explanation: 429 plus Retry-After tells well-behaved clients exactly when to come back, which stops retry storms. A 500 invites more retries and a 200 lies.

questions.prompt: Traffic is 10× normal and every gateway checks a single Redis shard for every request. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: The single Redis shard holding the counters

questions.explanation: Every request costs a Redis round trip on one shard. Shard counters by key, or keep local token buckets that sync periodically.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism lets many gateways enforce one user's limit consistently?

choices.label: A SQL row lock taken on every single request
The client counts its own requests and reports them
An atomic token-bucket update in Redis via a Lua script
Each gateway keeps its own counter and never shares it

questions.explanation: A Lua script runs the read-check-decrement atomically in Redis, so concurrent gateways cannot both spend the last token. Local-only counters let a user exceed the limit N times over.

questions.prompt: Redis, which holds the rate-limit counters, goes down. For a login endpoint under attack, what is the safer default?

choices.label: Restart every gateway until Redis comes back
Fail open for login, so legitimate users are never blocked
Fail closed for login, so attackers cannot brute-force freely
Switch all limits off globally until someone is paged

questions.explanation: For security-sensitive endpoints, failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is safer; for ordinary reads, failing open keeps the product up.

steps: Peak ≈ 4,630 × 5 ≈ 23,000 API calls per second (the quiz target is about 23,000).

steps: The API gateway calls the limiter before routing each request, with keys such as user id, phone number, API key and IP range.
The limiter runs a Lua script in Redis that refills and takes a token atomically (token bucket), so concurrent servers cannot both take the last token.
If the bucket is empty, the gateway returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header and RateLimit headers.
Rules are stored in a config service and pushed to gateways; changes take effect without deploys.
If Redis is unavailable, the gateway falls back to a conservative local in-memory limit per instance (fail open with a cap) for most APIs, and fails closed for OTP sends.

title: Unique ID Generator
objectives: Scope Unique ID Generator: generate unique 64-bit ids on demand, ids roughly sortable by time
Size it: 1B IDs/day, about 35,000/s at peak
Defend the design: each generator node has a unique worker id (snowflake: timestamp + worker + sequence)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 78 · Unique ID Generator: Generate unique, roughly time-sortable 64-bit ids for orders, messages and payments across data centres. In scope: Generate unique 64-bit IDs on demand; IDs roughly sortable by time; Work across many data centres.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 78 non-functionals: Under 1 ms per ID. No duplicates, ever. No single point of failure. Out of scope: Human-readable vanity IDs; Cryptographic secrecy of IDs.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 78 reference path: Each generator node has a unique worker ID (Snowflake: timestamp + worker + sequence). → Clock moving backwards is detected and the node waits or refuses. → No central counter on the hot path.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 78 risks: Clock skew: NTP corrections can move clocks backwards; issuing ids then could repeat a timestamp with a reused sequence. Alternatives: UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128 bits and random, which hurts B-tree locality; UUIDv7 is time-ordered and standard; database ranges (ticket servers) are simple but depend on a central database.

questions.prompt: A service calls nextId() and the call fails halfway. What makes retrying safe?

choices.label: Reuse the previous id if the call looked like it failed
Store every issued id in a database before returning it
Ask the clock service for permission before each retry
Nothing extra: a fresh id is unique, so an unused one is just skipped

questions.explanation: Snowflake ids are cheap and unique; losing one leaves a gap, which is harmless. Reusing ids would risk collisions.

questions.prompt: Id demand rises 10× and ids come from one central id service. What saturates first?
questions.explanation: A central service is a hot spot and a single point of failure. Embedding the generator as a library with leased worker ids removes the network hop entirely.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism keeps ids unique across 1,024 workers without coordination per id?

choices.label: A global counter incremented in SQL for each id
A unique worker id in each 64-bit id, plus timestamp and sequence
Random 64-bit numbers with no structure at all
The hostname hashed into the lower bits each time

questions.explanation: Timestamp, worker id and a per-millisecond sequence make each id unique by construction; the worker id is leased once at startup.

questions.prompt: A server's clock jumps backwards by 2 seconds. What should the generator do?

choices.label: Refuse to issue ids until the clock passes the last timestamp
Reset the sequence to zero and carry on regardless
Keep issuing ids with the earlier timestamp as normal
Switch to random ids until somebody restarts it

questions.explanation: Issuing with an older timestamp can repeat ids already handed out. Waiting (or failing fast) preserves uniqueness.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for Unique ID Generator?
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Under 1 ms per ID; No duplicates, ever; No single point of failure. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: Unique ID Generator: assume about 1B IDs a day, with traffic peaking at 3× the daily average. Estimate peak IDs per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 1B IDs/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 12,000/s on average; × 3 peak ≈ 35,000/s.

questions.prompt: A service calls nextId() and the call fails halfway. What makes retrying safe?

choices.label: Reuse the previous id if the call looked like it failed
Store every issued id in a database before returning it
Ask the clock service for permission before each retry
Nothing extra: a fresh id is unique, so an unused one is just skipped

questions.explanation: Snowflake ids are cheap and unique; losing one leaves a gap, which is harmless. Reusing ids would risk collisions.

questions.prompt: Id demand rises 10× and ids come from one central id service. What saturates first?
questions.explanation: A central service is a hot spot and a single point of failure. Embedding the generator as a library with leased worker ids removes the network hop entirely.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism keeps ids unique across 1,024 workers without coordination per id?

choices.label: A global counter incremented in SQL for each id
A unique worker id in each 64-bit id, plus timestamp and sequence
Random 64-bit numbers with no structure at all
The hostname hashed into the lower bits each time

questions.explanation: Timestamp, worker id and a per-millisecond sequence make each id unique by construction; the worker id is leased once at startup.

questions.prompt: A server's clock jumps backwards by 2 seconds. What should the generator do?

choices.label: Refuse to issue ids until the clock passes the last timestamp
Reset the sequence to zero and carry on regardless
Keep issuing ids with the earlier timestamp as normal
Switch to random ids until somebody restarts it

questions.explanation: Issuing with an older timestamp can repeat ids already handed out. Waiting (or failing fast) preserves uniqueness.

bossDeep.pitch: Generate unique, roughly time-sortable 64-bit ids for orders, messages and payments across data centres.

assumptions: Snowflake layout: 41-bit milliseconds, 10-bit worker id, 12-bit sequence
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 IDs per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
One worker can issue 4,096 ids per millisecond, about 4,096,000 per second.
Peak demand of about 35,000 per second needs only one worker in theory; run several per data centre for availability.
10 worker bits allow 1,024 workers, for example 5 bits of data centre and 5 bits of machine.
capacity.result: About 35,000 ids per second at peak is tiny compared with one Snowflake worker's 4 million per second; the real requirements are uniqueness and no single point of failure.

steps: Each generator process gets a unique worker id at start-up, leased from ZooKeeper or etcd, or assigned by deployment config.
To generate: read the clock in milliseconds; if it equals the last timestamp, increment the sequence, otherwise reset it to 0; if the sequence overflows, wait for the next millisecond.
Compose the id from the timestamp shifted left 22 bits, the worker id shifted left 12, and the sequence.
Services usually embed the generator as a library, so there is no network call; a small id service is an alternative for languages without the library.
If the clock goes backwards, refuse or wait until it passes the last timestamp, and alert.
architecture.diagram:
service --(library)--> [ timestamp | worker id | sequence ] -> 64-bit id
worker id lease <- etcd/ZooKeeper (unique per process)

deepDives.title: Clock skew
deepDives.body: NTP corrections can move clocks backwards; issuing ids then could repeat a timestamp with a reused sequence. Waiting or failing fast is safer than risking a duplicate.

deepDives.title: Alternatives
deepDives.body: UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128 bits and random, which hurts B-tree locality; UUIDv7 is time-ordered and standard; database ranges (ticket servers) are simple but depend on a central database.

rubric: Explains the bit layout and its capacity.
Guarantees unique worker ids through a lease or config.
Handles clock rollback explicitly.
Avoids a central bottleneck on the hot path.

questions.prompt: A put(key, value) times out and the client retries. How does the store avoid a lost or doubled update?

choices.label: Append both values so nothing is ever lost at all
Ignore the retry because timeouts always mean failure
Send the version context; the retry overwrites the same version
Lock the key across all replicas before every write

questions.explanation: With version vectors the retried write carries the same context, so replicas treat it as one update. A timeout does not mean failure.

questions.prompt: One hot cart key gets 10× normal writes. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: The three replicas that own that key

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing sends every write for a key to the same replica set. Spread hot keys by splitting them or caching reads.

questions.prompt: A replica is down during a write with W=2. Which mechanism keeps the write and repairs the replica later?

choices.label: Reject every write until all three replicas are back
Hinted handoff to another node, replayed when the replica returns
Ask the client to resend once the replica recovers
Write to one node only and skip the others forever

questions.explanation: Another node stores the write with a hint and hands it over on recovery; read repair and Merkle anti-entropy fix anything left.

questions.prompt: Carts must never lose an item, even if two devices update at once. Which conflict policy fits?

choices.label: Last write wins using each server's wall clock
Keep siblings with version vectors and merge them on read
Pick whichever replica answered first and drop others
Reject the second write with an error to the user

questions.explanation: Last-write-wins silently drops one device's item. Keeping both versions and merging (union of items) matches the cart's needs.

steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 3 ≈ 17,000 operations per second (the quiz target is about 17,000).

steps: Partition keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes; each key lives on the next N = 3 distinct nodes on the ring.
Any node can coordinate a request: writes go to all 3 replicas and succeed after W acknowledgements; reads ask R replicas (QUORUM: R = 2, W = 2).

Conflicts are detected with version vectors or resolved with last-writer-wins timestamps, chosen per use case.

 W=2 acks -> ok   |   R=2 replies -> newest wins -> read repair
 gossip membership | hinted handoff | Merkle anti-entropy

questions.prompt: An app server sets a key with TTL, times out, and retries. What happens?

choices.label: The TTL doubles because both writes add time
The cache crashes because of duplicate keys
The value is stored twice and must be cleaned up
Nothing harmful: SET is idempotent, the same value is written again

questions.explanation: SET overwrites; repeating it is harmless. That is why caches can retry writes freely.

questions.prompt: A flash sale sends 10× reads for one product key. What saturates first?

questions.prompt: Many keys expire at the same moment and the database is flooded. Which mechanism prevents it?

choices.label: Set every TTL to exactly the same value for neatness
Add random jitter to TTLs and use single-flight on misses
Disable expiry so values are never refreshed at all
Let every request rebuild the value in parallel

questions.explanation: Jitter spreads expiries over time and single-flight lets one request rebuild while others wait or get stale data.

questions.prompt: Product prices change and must not stay wrong for long. Which write policy fits?

choices.label: Update the database, then delete the cache key
Never invalidate; rely only on a 24-hour TTL
Write the cache and the database in random order
Update the cache first and the database a day later

questions.explanation: Delete-after-write (cache-aside) bounds staleness to the brief window before the next read refills the key.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 81 · Notification System: Send push, SMS and email for an e-commerce app, including sale-time spikes. In scope: Send push/SMS/email; User preferences & opt-out; Retry failed deliveries.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.body: Boss 81 reference path: Services publish notification events to a queue. → Channel workers call SMS/push/email providers with retries and DLQ. → Preferences + dedupe store; per-user rate limits.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 81 risks: Not spamming users: Frequency caps per user per day, dedup by idempotency key and quiet hours (no promotional pushes at 2 AM) matter as much as throughput. assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 20 video segment requests each per day
This quiz scenario is deliberately small; real viewing generates hundreds of segment requests per hour watched
steps: Daily video segment requests = 50,000,000 × 20 = 1,000,000,000.
Peak ≈ 11,600 × 4 ≈ 46,000 video segment requests per second (the quiz target is about 46,000).
Segment egress at about 46,000 requests per second × 1 MB is about 46,000 MB per second, about 368 Gbit per second.

Resume points are tiny writes, for example one every 30 seconds per active viewer, stored in a key-value store.
capacity.result: About 46,000 segment requests per second already means hundreds of Gbit per second: delivery is a CDN problem, the control plane is ordinary services.

steps: The catalogue and personalised rows are served by stateless services and caches from the control-plane region.
Pressing play fetches a manifest listing renditions and segment URLs on the nearest CDN or ISP cache.
The player downloads segments, measuring throughput and switching bitrate to keep the buffer healthy.
The player reports progress periodically; a key-value store keeps (user, title) → position for resume on any device.
Control-plane services run in more than one region with failover; content is pre-positioned at edges overnight.

app -> catalogue/personalisation (control plane, multi-region)
play -> manifest -> segments from ISP/edge cache (adaptive)
progress -> KV store (user, title) -> resume

title: Uber/Ola
objectives: Scope Uber/Ola: request a ride, match nearby driver
Size it: 80M ride requests/day, about 3,700/s at peak
Defend the design: drivers stream locations via websocket into a geo index (geohash in redis)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 88 · Uber/Ola: Uber or Ola: match riders with nearby drivers in Indian cities and track trips live. In scope: Request a ride; Match nearby driver; Live location tracking.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 88 non-functionals: Match < 5 s. Location updates every 4 s. No double assignment. Out of scope: Fare surge pricing model details; Driver onboarding and KYC.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 88 reference path: Drivers stream locations via WebSocket into a geo index (geohash in Redis). → Matching service queries nearby drivers and locks one with CAS. → Trips in SQL; surge via stream processing.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 88 risks: No double assignment: A conditional update on the ride row, or a compare-and-set on the driver's status, guarantees one winner even if two acceptances arrive together. Hot zones: Airports and stations at peak overload a few cells; finer cells and per-zone dispatch partitions keep queries fast.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 4 ride requests each per day
500,000 online drivers sending a location every 4 seconds
steps: Daily ride requests = 20,000,000 × 4 = 80,000,000.
Average = 80,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 926 per second.
Peak ≈ 926 × 4 ≈ 3,700 ride requests per second (the quiz target is about 3,700).
Location writes = 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 per second, larger than ride requests.
Each update is about 100 bytes, so about 12.5 MB per second of location ingest.
Only the latest position matters for matching, so it lives in memory; history goes to a stream for analytics.
capacity.result: Ride requests peak around 3,700 per second, but location updates reach about 125,000 per second: the geo index is the hot path.

steps: Drivers stream locations over a persistent connection to location gateways, which update an in-memory geo index (geohash or H3 cell → drivers) partitioned by city.
A ride request goes to the dispatch service, which reads nearby cells, filters available drivers and ranks by estimated arrival time.
Dispatch offers the ride to one driver at a time (or a few in sequence) with a short timeout.
Acceptance uses a conditional write on the ride (status = requested → assigned) so two drivers cannot both get it.
During the trip, driver locations are forwarded to the rider's app; trip events go to Kafka for billing and analytics.

driver app -> location gateway -> geo index (city shard, cells) 
rider -> dispatch -> nearby cells -> rank by ETA -> offer -> accept (conditional write)
trip events -> Kafka -> billing, analytics

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 89 · Zomato/Swiggy: Zomato or Swiggy: browse restaurants, order and pay, and track the delivery rider live. In scope: Browse & search restaurants; Place order & pay; Track rider live.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 89 risks: Order state consistency: An explicit state machine (placed → paid → accepted → picked → delivered) in SQL, changed only by valid transitions, prevents impossible states. A saga compensation: cancel and refund the payment

bossDeep.pitch: Zomato or Swiggy: browse restaurants, order and pay, and track the delivery rider live.

assumptions: 30 million daily users, about 1 orders each per day
Menus are read about 50 times per order
steps: Average = 30,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 347 per second.
Peak ≈ 347 × 6 ≈ 2,100 orders per second (the quiz target is about 2,100).

Rider location updates add a geo workload similar to ride-hailing.

cards.title: The brief

steps: The client splits files into chunks and hashes each one (SHA-256).

The metadata service publishes a change event; other devices, connected by long-polling or WebSocket, fetch the changed file list and download only missing chunks.

commit version (SQL) -> change event -> other devices sync -> download missing chunks

cards.title: The brief

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 92 risks: Exactly-once debit: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit. choices.label: It removes the need for a database
States like PENDING and DEEMED make timeouts and late callbacks explicit

bossDeep.pitch: A UPI-style payment app (PSP) on top of NPCI: pay to a VPA, collect requests and history.

assumptions: 150 million daily users, about 3 transactions each per day
Each transaction writes about 5 ledger and state rows of 500 bytes
Peak days such as festivals add more; UPI volumes are publicly reported by NPCI monthly
steps: Peak ≈ 5,210 × 5 ≈ 26,000 transactions per second (the quiz target is about 26,000).
Daily transactions = 450,000,000; storage ≈ 450,000,000 × 2,500 bytes = 1,125,000,000,000 bytes, about 1.1 TB per day.
Peak of about 26,000 transactions per second needs a sharded transaction store, for example by payer id.
Every transaction involves calls to NPCI and banks, so most latency is external; the app must handle timeouts and pending states.
capacity.result: About 26,000 transactions per second with external dependencies: idempotency, a clear state machine and reconciliation matter more than raw speed.

steps: The app creates a transaction with a unique transaction reference (idempotency key) and status INITIATED in a SQL ledger sharded by user.
The PSP sends the request to NPCI, which routes the debit to the payer's bank and the credit to the payee's bank.
Responses move the state machine (INITIATED → PENDING → SUCCESS or FAILED); retries reuse the same reference, so no double debit.
Timeouts leave the transaction PENDING; a status-check job queries NPCI and a reconciliation job compares daily settlement files.
History is served from a read model; every state change is written to an append-only audit log.
architecture.diagram:
app -> PSP txn svc (unique txn ref, SQL ledger) -> NPCI -> payer bank (debit) / payee bank (credit)
responses -> state machine | timeouts -> status check | daily recon files

deepDives.title: Exactly-once debit
deepDives.body: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit.

deepDives.title: Pending states
deepDives.body: Network timeouts are common; showing 'pending, we will update you' and resolving via status checks is safer than guessing success or failure.

rubric: Uses a unique transaction reference end to end.
Models an explicit state machine including PENDING.
Reconciles with settlement files.
Keeps an append-only audit trail.

title: BookMyShow
objectives: Scope BookMyShow: view shows & seat map, hold seats for 10 min
Size it: 50M seat views/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: seat holds via conditional update or short redis lock with ttl

cards.title: The brief

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 94 risks: Double booking: Because the hold only succeeds when the seat is FREE in the same statement, two users clicking the same seat cannot both succeed. 10,000 units of a phone, 5,000,000 users waiting at 12:00 (illustrative)

steps: Sale pages and assets are static and served by a CDN; the countdown uses client time synced to the server.
At sale start, a waiting room issues signed tokens and admits users at a controlled rate; rate limits and bot checks apply per account and device.

A reservation creates an order with a short payment window; unpaid reservations expire and return stock.
Once stock reaches zero, the sale page flips to sold out at the edge, so later requests never reach the backend.

users -> CDN (static) -> waiting room (tokens, rate limit) -> reserve: atomic decrement (stock buckets) -> order -> pay
expired -> stock back | sold out -> edge page

functional: Match buy and sell orders by price-time priority
Publish trades and order book updates

assumptions: About 5,000 listed symbols, with trading concentrated in a few hundred
Market hours about 6 hours and 15 minutes (as on NSE, publicly documented)
steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 10 ≈ 58,000 orders per second (the quiz target is about 58,000).
The quiz scenario's daily average is about 5,800 orders per second over 24 hours; over a 6.25-hour session the real average would be about 22,000 per second, before bursts.
With a 10× peak factor, about 58,000 orders per second across all symbols; the busiest symbol may take a large share.
One single-threaded matching engine handles hundreds of thousands of simple operations per second in memory, so one engine per symbol (or per group) fits.
capacity.result: About 58,000 orders per second at peak: deterministic in-memory matching per symbol, with a durable sequenced log for recovery and audit.

steps: Orders arrive through gateways that validate them and run risk checks (margin, limits).
A sequencer assigns a global sequence number and writes each order to a replicated log before matching.
A single-threaded matching engine per symbol keeps the order book in memory: buy and sell sides sorted by price, then time; incoming orders match against the best opposite prices.
Trades and book updates are published to market-data feeds and to clearing; every event is in the log.
Hot standby engines replay the same log; on failure, a standby with the same state takes over deterministically.

traders -> gateways (validate, risk) -> sequencer (seq no, replicated log) -> matching engine per symbol (in-memory book)
 -> trades -> clearing | book updates -> market data | standby replays log

steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 4 ≈ 930 joins per second (the quiz target is about 930).
Mesh peer-to-peer: each participant uploads to 9 others, so 9 × 1.5 = 13.5 megabits per second of upload, too much for most home connections in India.
SFU: each participant uploads once (1.5 megabits per second, or several simulcast layers) and downloads 9 streams.
Joins at about 930 per second are light signalling; media bandwidth through SFUs is the real capacity driver.
capacity.result: Joins are only about 930 per second, but media is heavy: SFUs in regions near users forward streams and adapt quality.

steps: Clients join via a signalling service over WebSocket, which authenticates them and assigns a room to a nearby regional SFU.
Media uses WebRTC over UDP with STUN and TURN for NAT traversal; TURN relays when direct UDP is blocked.
Each client sends simulcast layers (for example 180p, 360p and 720p); the SFU forwards to each receiver the layer that fits its bandwidth and window size.
Screen share is another stream, prioritised for clarity over frame rate.
Large webinars switch to a broadcast model where a few speakers are forwarded to many viewers, possibly via a CDN with HLS for very large audiences.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 30 segment requests each per day
This quiz scenario is deliberately small; live viewers request a new segment every few seconds
Disney+ Hotstar publicly reported 25.3 million peak concurrent viewers in 2019
steps: Daily segment requests = 50,000,000 × 30 = 1,500,000,000.
Peak ≈ 17,400 × 4 ≈ 69,000 segment requests per second (the quiz target is about 69,000).
At a 4-second segment length, 25,000,000 viewers request about 25,000,000 ÷ 4 = 6,250,000 segments per second at peak.
At an average 2 megabits per second per viewer, egress is 25,000,000 × 2 = 50,000,000 megabits per second, which is 50 terabits per second.
Only multiple CDNs with edges deep inside Indian ISPs can deliver that; the origin must see a tiny fraction.
capacity.result: Real live peaks reach millions of segment requests and tens of Tbit per second: delivery is entirely a multi-CDN problem, with control-plane services pre-scaled for the toss.

steps: The live feed is encoded into an adaptive bitrate ladder and packaged into short HLS or DASH segments within seconds.
Segments go to an origin with an origin shield, then to multiple CDNs; manifests point players at the best CDN for their ISP and region.
Players fetch segments adaptively, dropping quality on weak 4G instead of buffering.
Login, entitlement and ad services are pre-scaled before the match, because many users join within minutes of the toss.
Non-essential features (comments, recommendations) degrade first under stress; playback is protected.

camera feed -> encoders (ABR ladder) -> packager (segments) -> origin + shield -> multi-CDN edges -> players
login/entitlement/ads: pre-scaled | degrade extras first

assumptions: 2 million daily users, about 10 submissions each per day
Each submission takes about 2 seconds of sandbox time
steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 10 ≈ 2,300 submissions per second (the quiz target is about 2,300).
Peak of about 2,300 submissions per second × 2 seconds = 4,600 sandbox-seconds per second, so about 4,600 sandboxes busy at once.
If one worker machine runs 16 sandboxes, that is about 4,600 ÷ 16 ≈ 288 machines at contest peak.
Outside contests the fleet can scale down to a small fraction of that.
capacity.result: About 2,300 submissions per second at contest peak needs thousands of concurrent sandboxes: queue, isolate and autoscale.

steps: The API stores the submission and puts a job on a queue (separate queues per contest for fairness).
Workers pull jobs and run code in sandboxes (containers or microVMs such as gVisor or Firecracker) with no network, CPU and memory limits, time limits and a read-only filesystem.
Tests run against hidden inputs; outputs are compared and a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit) is produced.
Verdicts are written back and pushed to the user; contest leaderboards update from verdict events.
Workers autoscale on queue depth before and during contests.
architecture.diagram:
submit -> API (store) -> queue (per contest) -> workers -> sandbox (no network, limits) -> verdict
verdict -> DB -> push to user | events -> leaderboard

nonFunctional: Counts may lag by a few seconds

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 20 increments each per day
A viral post receives 50,000 increments per second (illustrative)
One Redis key handles roughly 100,000 simple increments per second on one core (illustrative)
steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 5 ≈ 120,000 increments per second (the quiz target is about 120,000).
Peak overall is about 120,000 increments per second across all counters, easily spread over a cluster.
One viral counter at 50,000 per second sits uncomfortably close to a single key's limit and its shard's CPU.
Splitting it into 32 sub-counters gives about 50,000 ÷ 32 ≈ 1,560 increments per second each.
capacity.result: About 120,000 increments per second overall, with single hot counters near one key's limit: shard hot counters and sum on read.

steps: Increments go to a counter service, which writes to Redis with INCR on the counter key, or on one of N sub-keys chosen at random for hot counters.
Reads sum the N sub-counters (cached for a second or two), so counts may lag slightly.
Increments are also written to a log (Kafka) so counts can be rebuilt and persisted to a durable store periodically.
Counters become hot automatically: when a key's rate passes a threshold, the service starts spreading it over more sub-keys.
Duplicate increments (such as a double like) are prevented by storing the like itself with a unique (user, post) constraint; the counter counts accepted likes.

read -> sum 32 sub-keys (cache 1 s) | log -> Kafka -> durable store

mechanism.title: The first five minutes, step by step
steps: Restate the problem in one sentence to confirm scope: 'A service where riders request autos and nearby drivers accept, in one country, mobile apps only.'
Functional requirements: list 3–5 core user actions and agree which are in scope (request ride, match driver, track trip, pay) and which are out (ratings, scheduled rides, chat).
Non-functional requirements: ask for scale (daily active users, peak factor), latency targets, availability, consistency needs per feature, durability, and regional or regulatory constraints.
Write explicit assumptions where the interviewer has no preference: '10 million DAU, peak 3× average, 99.9% availability, match within 5 seconds at p99.'
Turn assumptions into anchor numbers you will reuse: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Do the arithmetic aloud and round sensibly.
Confirm priorities: 'I'll focus on matching and location updates, and treat payments as a black box unless you want me to go there.'

useWhen: Always, in the first few minutes, before drawing any boxes.
Again whenever the interviewer adds a twist ('now make it work offline'): restate the changed requirement before redesigning.
avoidWhen: Do not spend more than about 5 minutes of a 45-minute interview on requirements; move on with stated assumptions.
Do not ask questions you will not use; every number you gather should change a design decision.

rows: How many daily users? Peak factor?
How fast must a match feel?
Can two drivers accept one ride?
Conditional writes or locks on the ride

numbers.title: Turning assumptions into anchor numbers
assumptions: 10 million DAU; each user makes 2 ride requests per day
steps: Average per second = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231.
Peak per second = 231 × 3 = 693, call it about 700.
Driver location pings: 500,000 online drivers every 4 seconds gives 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 writes per second, far larger than ride requests, so location ingestion is the scaling hot spot.
numbers.result: Anchor numbers show that location pings, not ride requests, dominate load, which tells you where to spend the deep dive.

india.title: Clarifying a 'design an IRCTC-like booking system' prompt
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: If asked to design a train-booking system for India, strong candidates first separate normal booking from the Tatkal window, when demand spikes sharply at the opening minute. They ask whether the focus is search, seat inventory or payments, whether waitlist and RAC (reservation against cancellation) rules are in scope, and what consistency is required: a berth must never be sold twice, so seat allocation is strongly consistent while availability displays can be slightly stale. Stating 'I'll assume a burst of a few lakh booking attempts in the first minute, an illustrative estimate' lets them size queues and inventory locks instead of guessing later.

pitfalls.trap: Jumping straight to drawing a load balancer and a database.
pitfalls.say: 'Before designing, let me confirm the core features and the scale, so I size the right parts.'

pitfalls.trap: Collecting numbers and never using them.
pitfalls.say: 'At about 700 peak ride requests per second but 125,000 location writes per second, I'll focus the design on location ingestion.'

Ask only questions that change design decisions.
Write assumptions down and turn them into anchor numbers.
Use the numbers to choose where to deep-dive.

mechanism.title: Running a deep dive
steps: Pick the component where the requirements are hardest: the hot path at peak, the strongest consistency need, or the biggest data volume. Say why you picked it.
State the problem precisely: 'Two drivers can accept the same ride within milliseconds; we must allow exactly one.'
Offer two or three options, each in one sentence.
Compare with the trade-off template: 'Option A gives X at the cost of Y; option B gives Y but costs Z. Given our requirement W, I choose A.'
Go one level deeper on the chosen option: data model, the exact query or write, failure cases, and the numbers it must handle.
Close the loop: name what would make you switch options later (for example, 'if accepts exceed 10,000 per second on one city partition, I'd split by zone').

useWhen: Whenever you choose a technology or pattern, and whenever the interviewer asks 'why not X?'.
On the one or two components that carry the most risk; depth beats breadth.
avoidWhen: Do not deep-dive into something generic, like the load balancer algorithm, while the hard problem (matching, consistency) stays vague.
Do not use absolutes such as 'always use Kafka' or 'NoSQL is faster'; tie every claim to a requirement.

rows: 'X fits because we need ...; the cost is ...'
'It scales to about N per second per node; we need M, so about M ÷ N nodes'
'Cache menus for 5 minutes, invalidate on edit; prices at checkout from the database'
'Strong for ride acceptance, eventual for driver locations shown on the map'

numbers.title: Comparing two options with numbers
assumptions: Ride accept rate at peak 700 per second across a city
Option A: conditional update on the ride row in Postgres, about 2 ms each
Option B: a Redis lock per ride, about 0.5 ms each plus lock expiry handling
steps: Option A load: 700 writes per second, each touching one row, which one Postgres primary handles comfortably.
Total busy time for option A = 700 × 2 ms = 1,400 ms of work per second, spread over many connections and cores.
Option B is faster per call but adds a second system whose failover can drop locks, plus a lease to manage.
Since option A meets the load with the source of truth, choose A and mention B only if accepts grow 10× or more.
numbers.result: Use numbers to show the simpler option is enough, and name the threshold at which you would switch.

india.title: Deep dive on Tatkal seat allocation
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: In a train-booking interview, the right deep dive is seat allocation during the Tatkal opening, not the search page. A good answer compares a queue in front of the inventory service (fair and smooth, but adds waiting time), conditional decrements per train-class-date row (simple and strongly consistent, but one hot row per popular train), and pre-splitting a train's quota into several counters (more parallelism, slightly more complex rebalancing). The candidate then picks, for example, a queue plus conditional decrements, explains the failure cases (payment fails, hold expires and the seat returns), and states the illustrative load the design must take.

pitfalls.trap: 'Cassandra is better than Postgres.'
pitfalls.say: 'For ride acceptance we need a conditional write on one row; Postgres does that at 700 per second easily, so I'd keep it there.'

pitfalls.trap: Diving into a generic component.
pitfalls.say: 'The hard part here is double acceptance, so I'll go deep on that rather than load-balancer algorithms.'

takeaways: Deep-dive where the requirements are hardest.
Use 'X gives A at the cost of B; given W, I choose X'.
Replace absolutes with numbers and requirements.
Say what would make you change your mind.

title: Common Mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common design-interview mistakes
Keep designs proportional to the numbers

cards.title: Designing before scoping
cards.body: Drawing boxes before knowing scale or features. Everything after rests on guesses.

mechanism.title: How common mistakes unfold, and how to catch them
steps: No scope: the candidate starts drawing before agreeing on features and scale, then designs the wrong thing for 20 minutes.
Over-engineering: Kafka, microservices, multi-region active-active and a service mesh for a system with 50 requests per second.
Unused numbers: the estimate says 2 TB per year, then the design ignores it (or contradicts it by sharding across 100 nodes).
Silence: long stretches of thinking without speaking, so the interviewer cannot follow or help.
Ignoring hints: the interviewer asks 'what if two users book the same seat?' and the candidate moves on.

Recovery: when you notice any of these, say so plainly ('I over-built this; at 50 requests per second one service and Postgres are enough'), simplify and continue. Correcting yourself is a positive signal.

useWhen: Use this list as a self-check every ten minutes: scope agreed? numbers used? speaking aloud? following hints?
Use the recovery script whenever you realise you are off track.
avoidWhen: Do not hide a mistake and hope the interviewer misses it; they almost never do.
Do not overcorrect into designing nothing; keep a working end-to-end design on the board.

rows: Restate and agree core features first
Tie each component to a number
Narrate the options you are weighing
Treat a repeated question as the priority

numbers.title: Is Kafka justified here?
assumptions: Internal tool: 5,000 users, each creating 20 events per day
Kafka cluster minimum: 3 brokers, plus operations effort
steps: Events per day = 5,000 × 20 = 100,000.
Average per second = 100,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.2.
Even at a 10× peak that is about 12 events per second, which a Postgres table or a simple managed queue handles easily.
A three-broker Kafka cluster adds cost and on-call load for no benefit at this scale.
numbers.result: About 1 event per second does not need Kafka; matching tools to numbers is the cure for over-engineering.

india.title: Over-building a college fest ticketing app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A candidate asked to design ticketing for a college fest in Kolkata, about 20,000 tickets sold over two weeks, proposes Kubernetes, Kafka, Cassandra and multi-region failover. The interviewer asks for the numbers: 20,000 tickets over 14 days is about 1,430 a day, and even if a quarter sell in the first hour, that is about 5,000 in an hour, around 1.4 per second. The strong recovery is: 'I over-built this. A single web app with Postgres, a unique constraint on seat ids, a payment gateway webhook and a CDN for the poster is enough; I'd add a queue only if launch traffic proves bursty.'

pitfalls.trap: Defending an over-built design when challenged.
pitfalls.say: 'You're right, at about 1.4 tickets per second this is over-built; let me simplify to one service and Postgres.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring a repeated question from the interviewer.
pitfalls.say: 'You've asked about double booking twice, so let me address it now: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) makes the second booking fail cleanly.'

pitfalls.trap: Long silent thinking.
pitfalls.say: 'I'm weighing a queue against direct writes; the queue smooths bursts but adds latency. Given our numbers, direct writes are fine.'

takeaways: Agree scope before designing.
Match every component to a number.
Think aloud; silence hides good reasoning.
Recover openly; self-correction is a strength.
